children.title: Box-Constrained Interval Optimization
children.top_down_role: Bounded-domain global optimization without general nonlinear constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Box-Constrained Interval Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines validated global minimization when the only feasible-set restriction is an initial compact box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=[\underline x,\overline x]\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and compact, and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\). The box-constrained global optimization problem is
\[f^*=\min_{x\in X}f(x),\qquad X^*=\{x\in X:f(x)=f^*\}.\]
An interval formulation supplies an inclusion enclosure \(F(B)\supseteq\{f(x):x\in B\}\) for every subbox \(B\subseteq X\). It is validated when all lower bounds, upper bounds, exclusions, and reported enclosures are computed with outward rounding, so the conclusions remain valid despite finite-precision arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a function over one compact box using outward-rounded interval range enclosures that rigorously support bounds, exclusions, and certified output.
assumptions_latex: \(X=[\underline x,\overline x]\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and compact.
\(f:X\to\mathbb R\) attains its minimum.
\(F(B)\) encloses the range of \(f\) on every subbox \(B\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\min_{x\in X}f(x)\) and \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\) are the value and solution set to be validated.

notation.meaning: interval enclosure of the objective range on box B
global minimum value and global minimizer set

children.title: Inequality-Constrained Interval Optimization
children.top_down_role: Validated global optimization over inequality-defined feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Inequality-Constrained Interval Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines validated global minimization over a box intersected with finitely many nonlinear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty compact box, with objective \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) and constraint functions \(g_i:X\to\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Define
\[S=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\le 0\ \text{for all }i\},\qquad f^*=\min_{x\in S}f(x).\]
A validated interval formulation provides outward-rounded enclosures \(F(B)\) and \(G_i(B)\) of the respective ranges on every subbox \(B\subseteq X\). In particular, \(\inf G_i(B)>0\) rigorously proves \(B\cap S=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize over a compact box subject to inequalities, using interval objective and constraint enclosures to certify bounds and discard infeasible boxes.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty compact box.
\(f\) and every \(g_i\) have valid interval range enclosures on subboxes of \(X\).
\(S\ne\varnothing\) and \(f\) attains its minimum on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\min\{f(x):x\in X,\ g_i(x)\le0\ \forall i\}\), with \(\inf G_i(B)>0\Rightarrow B\cap S=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: interval range enclosure for constraint i on B

children.title: Equality-Constrained Interval Optimization
children.top_down_role: Validated global optimization over implicit lower-dimensional feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Equality-Constrained Interval Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines validated global minimization on an implicit feasible set cut out by equality equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty compact box, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\). Define
\[S=\{x\in X:h(x)=0\},\qquad f^*=\min_{x\in S}f(x).\]
A validated interval formulation supplies an objective enclosure \(F(B)\) and component enclosures \(H_j(B)\supseteq\{h_j(x):x\in B\}\) for every subbox \(B\subseteq X\). If \(0\notin H_j(B)\) for some \(j\), then \(B\cap S=\varnothing\); boxes not excluded may require interval equation contractors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize on a compact equality-defined set, using interval equation enclosures and contractors to retain all possible feasible points and minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty compact box.
\(F\) and each \(H_j\) are valid outward-rounded range enclosures.
\(S\ne\varnothing\) and \(f\) attains its minimum on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\min\{f(x):x\in X,\ h(x)=0\}\), with \(0\notin H_j(B)\Rightarrow B\cap S=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: interval enclosure of equality component j on B

children.title: Mixed-Constraint Interval Optimization
children.top_down_role: Joint treatment of bounds, equalities, and inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Constraint Interval Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines validated global minimization with simultaneous bound, inequality, and equality restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty compact box, with \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), \(g:X\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\). The mixed-constraint problem is
\[f^*=\min_{x\in S}f(x),\qquad S=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\le0\ \forall i,\ h_j(x)=0\ \forall j\}.\]
A validated formulation encloses the ranges of \(f\), every \(g_i\), and every \(h_j\) on each subbox. A box is rigorously infeasible if some inequality enclosure has positive lower endpoint or some equality enclosure omits zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize over box bounds, inequalities, and equalities jointly, with outward-rounded enclosures certifying objective bounds and infeasible-box rejection.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty compact box.
\(f\), every \(g_i\), and every \(h_j\) admit valid interval range enclosures.
\(S\ne\varnothing\) and \(f\) attains its minimum on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\min\{f(x):x\in X,\ g(x)\le0,\ h(x)=0\}\), with all interval exclusions preserving \(S\).

children.title: Analytic Model Regimes
children.top_down_role: Model properties governing the availability and strength of interval bounds and local verification.

children.title: Smooth Factorable Models
children.top_down_role: Expression-based models supporting validated first- and second-order information.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Factorable Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a nodewise twice-differentiable factorable regime supporting validated values, gradients, and Hessians.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a box. A smooth factorable model on \(X\) is a finite expression graph whose leaves are variables or constants and whose internal nodes are arithmetic operations or elementary functions. Every intermediate expression is defined on \(X\), and each internal operation is twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of all argument values generated from \(X\). Suppose the interval implementations of these operations enclose their values and first and second derivatives with outward rounding. Then interval evaluation and interval automatic differentiation produce, for every subbox \(B\subseteq X\), enclosures
\[F(B)\supseteq\{f(x):x\in B\},\qquad G(B)\supseteq\{\nabla f(x):x\in B\},\qquad H(B)\supseteq\{\nabla^2 f(x):x\in B\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite expression graph whose operations are twice differentiable throughout all relevant intermediate ranges supports validated interval enclosures of its values, gradients, and Hessians.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a box.
Every intermediate operation is defined and twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of its argument range over \(X\).
Interval value and derivative implementations are inclusion-correct and use outward rounding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every subbox \(B\subseteq X\), \(F(B)\supseteq\{f(x):x\in B\}\), \(G(B)\supseteq\{\nabla f(x):x\in B\}\), and \(H(B)\supseteq\{\nabla^2 f(x):x\in B\}\).

children.title: Nonsmooth Interval Extensions
children.top_down_role: Enclosure-compatible nonsmooth models retained only to the extent needed by interval global search.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Nonsmooth interval extensions in the bibliography and related devices

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Interval Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the range-enclosure contract retained when classical derivatives need not exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be a possibly nonsmooth function on a box \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\). A nonsmooth interval extension is a map \(F\) from subboxes of \(X\) to scalar intervals satisfying
\[\{f(x):x\in B\}\subseteq F(B)\quad\text{for every subbox }B\subseteq X.\]
It is inclusion isotonic if \(B_1\subseteq B_2\) implies \(F(B_1)\subseteq F(B_2)\). Validated global search may use \(\inf F(B)\) as a rigorous lower bound without assuming that \(f\) has a classical gradient or Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth interval extension encloses every function value on each box and thereby provides rigorous lower bounds without classical derivatives.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a box.
\(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is well-defined but need not be differentiable.
Interval endpoints are computed with outward rounding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(B)\subseteq F(B)\) and hence \(\inf F(B)\le\inf_{x\in B}f(x)\) for every subbox \(B\subseteq X\).

children.title: Black-Box Enclosure Oracles
children.top_down_role: Models accessed through trusted range and derivative-range interfaces rather than explicit factorable expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Black-Box Enclosure Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the trusted enclosure interface for models whose internal expressions are unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a function \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) on a box \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\), a black-box enclosure oracle is a callable map \(\mathcal O\) that returns, for every representable subbox \(B\subseteq X\), an outward-rounded interval \(\mathcal O_f(B)\) satisfying
\[\{f(x):x\in B\}\subseteq\mathcal O_f(B).\]
When derivative information is advertised, it additionally returns interval vectors or matrices enclosing every existing gradient or Hessian value on \(B\). Correctness of global certificates depends only on these enclosure contracts, not on access to the oracle's internal representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trusted black-box oracle returns rigorous range and optional derivative-range enclosures for every queried box, without exposing an expression graph.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is defined on a box \(X\).
Every oracle result uses outward-rounded representable endpoints.
Any advertised derivative exists throughout the queried box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(B)\subseteq\mathcal O_f(B)\) for every queried \(B\subseteq X\), with analogous inclusion for each advertised derivative range.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The enclosure-oracle interface is plausible and internally coherent, but no citation supports the black-box contract, optional derivative interface, or representation-independence claim.

children.title: Certified Output Families
children.top_down_role: Distinct validated conclusions produced by a completed or tolerance-terminated search.

children.title: Global Optimum-Value Enclosures
children.top_down_role: Certified value intervals for the global optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Optimum-Value Enclosures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certifies a closed interval containing the attained global minimum value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq X\) be nonempty, let \(f^*=\min_{x\in S}f(x)\), and let \(\mathcal B\) be a finite box cover of \(S\). Suppose each \(B\in\mathcal B\) has a certified lower bound \(\ell_B\le\inf_{x\in B\cap S}f(x)\), and a certified feasible point \(\hat x\in S\) is known. Then
\[L=\min_{B\in\mathcal B}\ell_B,\qquad U=f(\hat x)\]
define a global optimum-value enclosure \([L,U]\), because \(L\le f^*\le U\). Its width \(U-L\) is a certified absolute optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certified box lower bounds and one feasible objective value produce an interval containing the global optimum and a rigorous absolute gap.
assumptions_latex: \(S\ne\varnothing\) and \(f\) attains \(f^*\) on \(S\).
\(\mathcal B\) is a finite cover of \(S\).
Each \(\ell_B\) and \(f(\hat x)\) is evaluated rigorously, with \(\hat x\in S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*\in[L,U]\) and \(0\le U-f^*\le U-L\).

notation.meaning: certified global lower and upper bounds
finite box cover of the feasible set

children.title: Global Minimizer Coverings
children.top_down_role: Certified box or subpaving covers containing every global minimizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Minimizer Coverings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certifies a finite box union containing every global minimizer, without asserting uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq X\), let \(f^*=\min_{x\in S}f(x)\), and let \(\mathcal C\) be a finite family of boxes. The family is a certified global-minimizer covering when
\[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x)\subseteq\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal C}B.\]
This inclusion is certified by an exhaustive partition of \(X\) if every terminal box outside \(\mathcal C\) is rigorously proved infeasible or is assigned a lower bound strictly exceeding a certified upper bound \(U\ge f^*\). The covering may contain nonminimizers and may overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite box family covers all global minimizers when exhaustive validation excludes every outside terminal box by infeasibility or an objective bound.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) attains its minimum on the feasible set \(S\subseteq X\).
Terminal boxes form a finite exhaustive cover of \(X\).
Every excluded box has a validated infeasibility or objective-bound certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x)\subseteq\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal C}B\).

notation.meaning: certified upper bound on the global minimum

children.title: Feasible-Set Subpavings
children.top_down_role: Inner, outer, boundary, and undecided box representations of feasible sets.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Subpavings; Characterizing Sets Defined by Inequalities

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Set Subpavings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a feasible set by classified boxes at a fixed resolution or stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq X\subset\mathbb R^n\), where \(X\) is a box. A feasible-set subpaving consists of finite, pairwise interior-disjoint box families \(\mathcal I\), \(\mathcal O\), and \(\mathcal U\) such that
\[\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal I}B\subseteq S\subseteq\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal I\cup\mathcal U}B,\qquad B\cap S=\varnothing\ \text{for every }B\in\mathcal O.\]
The inner boxes \(\mathcal I\) are certified feasible, the outer boxes \(\mathcal O\) are certified infeasible, and the undecided or boundary boxes \(\mathcal U\) contain every unresolved portion of \(S\). Their union covers the initial box \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subpaving partitions the search box into certified feasible, certified infeasible, and unresolved boundary boxes while providing inner and outer feasible-set approximations.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq X\subset\mathbb R^n\), with \(X\) a box.
\(\mathcal I\), \(\mathcal O\), and \(\mathcal U\) are finite and pairwise interior-disjoint.
\(X=\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal I\cup\mathcal O\cup\mathcal U}B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal I}B\subseteq S\subseteq\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal I\cup\mathcal U}B\) and \(\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal O}B\subseteq X\setminus S\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three-family representation is mathematically coherent, but no source establishes this particular inner/outer/undecided convention or its treatment of boundary boxes.

children.title: Complete Problem Infeasibility
children.top_down_role: Search-wide certification that the feasible region is empty.

knowledge_statements.title: Complete Problem Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certifies emptiness of the entire mixed-constraint feasible region by exhaustive box exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a box, let \(m,p\in\mathbb N\), and let \(g_i:X\to\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(h_j:X\to\mathbb R\) for \(j=1,\ldots,p\). Define
\[S=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\le0\ \text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m,\ h_j(x)=0\ \text{for every }j=1,\ldots,p\}.\]
Let \(\mathcal B\) be a finite box family covering \(X\). Suppose valid interval enclosures \(G_i(B)\supseteq\{g_i(x):x\in B\}\) and \(H_j(B)\supseteq\{h_j(x):x\in B\}\) are available for every \(B\in\mathcal B\). If, for each \(B\in\mathcal B\), either \(\inf G_i(B)>0\) for some \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), or \(0\notin H_j(B)\) for some \(j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\), then \(S=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every box in a finite cover of the search domain is excluded by a validated inequality or equality test, the entire mixed-constraint feasible set is empty.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is covered by the finite box family \(\mathcal B\).
For every relevant \(i\), \(j\), and \(B\), the intervals \(G_i(B)\) and \(H_j(B)\) are valid outward-rounded range enclosures.
Every \(B\in\mathcal B\) satisfies at least one stated interval exclusion test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: inequality and equality range enclosures on B

children.title: Scalar Interval Sets
children.top_down_role: Scalar interval forms, endpoints, widths, radii, and related set characteristics.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Interval Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines closed bounded real intervals, including singleton intervals, as scalar enclosure containers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty scalar interval is a closed bounded subset of \(\mathbb R\) determined by endpoints \(\underline a,\overline a\in\mathbb R\) with \(\underline a\le\overline a\):
\[[\underline a,\overline a]=\{x\in\mathbb R:\underline a\le x\le\overline a\}.\]
The collection of such intervals is \(\mathbb{IR}=\{[\underline a,\overline a]:\underline a\le\overline a\}\). Its width, midpoint, and radius are \(\overline a-\underline a\), \((\underline a+\overline a)/2\), and \((\overline a-\underline a)/2\), respectively. A singleton \([a,a]\) identifies the real number \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar interval is a closed bounded real set specified by ordered endpoints; singleton intervals canonically represent real numbers.
assumptions_latex: \(\underline a,\overline a\in\mathbb R\).
\(\underline a\le\overline a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([\underline a,\overline a]\in\mathbb{IR}\) and \(x\in[\underline a,\overline a]\iff\underline a\le x\le\overline a\).

notation.meaning: set of nonempty closed bounded real intervals
degenerate interval representing a real scalar

children.title: Cartesian Interval Boxes
children.top_down_role: Axis-aligned multidimensional interval containers used for search regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian Interval Boxes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines axis-aligned closed boxes in finite-dimensional real space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an integer \(n\ge 1\), let \(\underline{x},\overline{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(\underline{x}_i\le \overline{x}_i\) for every \(i\). The Cartesian interval box determined by these endpoints is
\[
X=[\underline{x},\overline{x}]:=\prod_{i=1}^n[\underline{x}_i,\overline{x}_i]=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\underline{x}_i\le x_i\le\overline{x}_i\text{ for all }i\}.
\]
Its width vector is \(w(X):=\overline{x}-\underline{x}\), and its midpoint is \(m(X):=(\underline{x}+\overline{x})/2\). A box is degenerate in coordinate \(i\) exactly when \(\underline{x}_i=\overline{x}_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Cartesian interval box is the product of finitely many closed real intervals, equivalently the set of vectors lying coordinatewise between specified lower and upper endpoints.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(n\ge 1\).
\(\underline{x},\overline{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\underline{x}\le\overline{x}\) componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X=\prod_{i=1}^n[\underline{x}_i,\overline{x}_i]\) is an axis-aligned closed subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: Cartesian interval box with componentwise endpoints

children.title: Interval Intersection Operations
children.top_down_role: Set contraction and overlap handling for scalar intervals or boxes.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Intersection Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes scalar-interval and Cartesian-box intersections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For closed real intervals \(I=[a,b]\) and \(J=[c,d]\), define \(\ell:=\max\{a,c\}\) and \(u:=\min\{b,d\}\). Then
\[
I\cap J=\begin{cases}[\ell,u],&\ell\le u,\\ \varnothing,&\ell>u.\end{cases}
\]
Consequently, if \(X=\prod_{i=1}^n I_i\) and \(Y=\prod_{i=1}^n J_i\), then \(X\cap Y=\prod_{i=1}^n(I_i\cap J_i)\) when every coordinate intersection is nonempty; if any coordinate intersection is empty, then \(X\cap Y=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersect intervals by taking the larger lower endpoint and smaller upper endpoint. Box intersection is coordinatewise and is empty if any coordinate intersection is empty.
assumptions_latex: \(I=[a,b]\) and \(J=[c,d]\) are nonempty closed real intervals.
\(X\) and \(Y\) are boxes of the same finite dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed endpoint formulas give the exact set intersections \(I\cap J\) and \(X\cap Y\).

notation.meaning: maximum of the two lower endpoints
minimum of the two upper endpoints

children.title: Interval Hull Operations
children.top_down_role: Hull-based enclosure of unions, point collections, and intermediate results.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Hull Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the least closed interval or box containing given bounded sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty bounded set \(S\subset\mathbb{R}\), its interval hull is
\[
\operatorname{hull}(S):=[\inf S,\sup S],
\]
the unique least closed real interval containing \(S\). In particular, for \(I=[a,b]\) and \(J=[c,d]\),
\[
\operatorname{hull}(I\cup J)=[\min\{a,c\},\max\{b,d\}].
\]
For a nonempty bounded set \(T\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), its box hull is \(\prod_{i=1}^n[\inf_{x\in T}x_i,\sup_{x\in T}x_i]\), the least Cartesian interval box containing \(T\) under set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interval hull is the smallest closed interval containing a bounded set; the box hull applies the same construction independently to every coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subset\mathbb{R}\) or \(T\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and bounded.
\(I=[a,b]\) and \(J=[c,d]\) are nonempty closed intervals when the binary formula is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{hull}(S)\) and the displayed box hull are the unique least interval containers under inclusion.

notation.meaning: least closed interval container of a scalar set
coordinate i of a vector x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Validated Interval Operation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Containment requirement and outward-rounding convention for implemented interval operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For input intervals \(X_1,\ldots,X_k\) and a corresponding point operation \(f\), an interval operation returns an interval \(F(X_1,\ldots,X_k)\) such that \[\{f(x_1,\ldots,x_k):x_i\in X_i\text{ and }f(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\text{ is defined}\}\subseteq F(X_1,\ldots,X_k).\] Implemented result intervals are rounded outward.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interval operation returns an interval containing every defined pointwise result obtainable from the input intervals. Implemented endpoints are rounded outward.

f(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\text{ is considered only where it is defined}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interval Operations, Natural Evaluation, and Centered Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval-hull definitions, natural interval evaluation accuracy, and the centered-form inclusion stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For interval boxes \(X=[\underline x,\bar x]\) and \(Y=[\underline y,\bar y]\), let \(\square S=[\inf S,\sup S]\) componentwise and define \(X\circ Y=\square\{x\circ y:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}\) whenever the pointwise operation is defined. Thus \(X+Y=[\underline x+\underline y,\bar x+\bar y]\), \(X-Y=[\underline x-\bar y,\bar x-\underline y]\), \(X Y=\square\{\underline x\underline y,\underline x\bar y,\bar x\underline y,\bar x\bar y\}\), and, when \(0\notin Y\), \(X/Y=\square\{\underline x/\underline y,\underline x/\bar y,\bar x/\underline y,\bar x/\bar y\}\). For an elementary function \(\varphi\), define \(\varphi(X)=\square\{\varphi(x):x\in X\}\) whenever defined. Under the regularity conditions for simple interval evaluation, \(\bar x-\underline x=O(\epsilon)\) implies both \(\operatorname{range}(f,X)\subseteq f(X)\) and \(f(X)\subseteq\operatorname{range}(f,X)+O(\epsilon)\). For \(x,\xi\in X\), a valid interval-gradient enclosure gives the centered-form inclusion \(f(x)\in f(\xi)+\nabla f(X)(x-\xi)\); under the additional regularity conditions referenced in the extract, centered forms can reduce enclosure excess to order \(O(\epsilon^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval operations and elementary-function images are defined as interval hulls of their pointwise images, subject to their domains; division requires the divisor interval to exclude zero. Natural interval evaluation contains the true range and, under the stated regularity conditions, has enclosure excess of first order in the box width. A centered form uses a center value and an interval-gradient enclosure, and under suitable additional conditions can attain second-order enclosure excess.
assumptions_latex: X=[\underline x,\bar x],\quad Y=[\underline y,\bar y].
\text{The relevant pointwise operations and elementary functions are defined on their operand intervals.}
0\notin Y\quad\text{for interval division.}
\bar x-\underline x=O(\epsilon)\quad\text{and the regularity conditions for simple interval evaluation hold.}
x,\xi\in X\quad\text{and }\nabla f(X)\text{ encloses the gradients needed for the centered form.}
\text{The additional regularity conditions required for the stated }O(\epsilon^2)\text{ centered-form accuracy hold.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\circ Y=\square\{x\circ y:x\in X,y\in Y\},\quad \operatorname{range}(f,X)\subseteq f(X)\subseteq\operatorname{range}(f,X)+O(\epsilon),\quad f(x)\in f(\xi)+\nabla f(X)(x-\xi).

knowledge_statements.title: Elementary Interval Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives exact or enclosing interval extensions of arithmetic and elementary functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty compact intervals \(X,Y\subset\mathbb{R}\), the exact set-based arithmetic result for \(\circ\in\{+,-,\times\}\) is represented by
\[
X\circ Y:=\operatorname{hull}\{x\circ y:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}.
\]
Division is defined analogously when \(0\notin Y\). For a real elementary function \(g:D\to\mathbb{R}\), an interval operation \(G\) is valid on \(X\subset D\) when
\[
\{g(x):x\in X\}\subseteq G(X).
\]
When \(g\) is continuous and monotone on \(X=[a,b]\), its exact interval image is \([\min\{g(a),g(b)\},\max\{g(a),g(b)\}]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval arithmetic encloses all pointwise arithmetic results. Elementary-function evaluators must contain the true image, with endpoint evaluation exact on continuous monotone branches.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty compact real intervals.
For division, \(0\notin Y\).
For endpoint evaluation, \(g\) is continuous and monotone on \(X\subset D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interval results contain every corresponding real arithmetic or elementary-function value over the input intervals.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegative integer power of a scalar interval
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Casewise interval image under a nonnegative integer power, using the convention \(X^0=[1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X=[a,b]\) with \(a\le b\) and \(n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), the interval-power operation is
\[
X^n=\begin{cases}
[1,1],&n=0,\\
[a^n,b^n],&n>0\text{ and }(a\ge0\text{ or }n\text{ is odd}),\\
[b^n,a^n],&n>0,\ b\le0,\ n\text{ even},\\
[0,a^n],&n>0,\ a<0<b,\ n\text{ even},\ -a>b,\\
[0,b^n],&n>0,\ a<0<b,\ n\text{ even},\ -a\le b.
\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Return [1,1] for exponent zero. For a positive exponent, preserve endpoint order when the interval is nonnegative or the exponent is odd; reverse it for a nonpositive interval with an even exponent. For an even power of an interval crossing zero, use zero as the lower endpoint and the larger powered endpoint magnitude as the upper endpoint.
assumptions_latex: X=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R
a\le b
n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X^n\text{ is given by the stated parity- and sign-dependent cases, with }X^0=[1,1].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Casewise interval enclosure for sine
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A real-arithmetic sine enclosure selected using interval width, endpoint sine values, and endpoint signs of the derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=[a,b]\), \(a\le b\), and \(s_x=\operatorname{sign}(\cos x)\). Define
\[
S(X)=\begin{cases}
[-1,1],&s_a\ne s_b\text{ and }b-a\ge2\pi,\\
[\min\{\sin a,\sin b\},1],&s_a\ne s_b,\ b-a<2\pi,\ s_a>0,\\
[-1,\max\{\sin a,\sin b\}],&s_a\ne s_b,\ b-a<2\pi,\ s_a\le0,\\
[-1,1],&s_a=s_b\text{ and }b-a\ge\pi,\\
[\sin a,\sin b],&s_a=s_b,\ b-a<\pi,\ s_a>0,\\
[\sin b,\sin a],&s_a=s_b,\ b-a<\pi,\ s_a\le0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(\sin(X)\subseteq S(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the signs of cosine at the interval endpoints together with the interval width to decide whether sine is monotone, crosses an extremum, or should receive the full enclosure [-1,1]. On monotone cases, order the endpoint sine values; when one extremum is covered, include 1 or -1 as appropriate.
assumptions_latex: X=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R
a\le b
s_x=\operatorname{sign}(\cos x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{\sin x:x\in[a,b]\}\subseteq S(X).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise interval-box arithmetic and its algebraic boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines componentwise sum, difference, product, and division for equal-dimensional boxes, while recording the stronger coordinatewise nonzero-denominator condition required by the displayed division formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For boxes \(B_j=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i^j,u_i^j]\), define
\[
B_1+B_2=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i^1+\ell_i^2,u_i^1+u_i^2],\qquad B_1-B_2=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i^1-u_i^2,u_i^1-\ell_i^2],
\]
\[
B_1*B_2=\prod_{i=1}^n[\min S_i,\max S_i],\quad S_i=\{\ell_i^1\ell_i^2,\ell_i^1u_i^2,u_i^1\ell_i^2,u_i^1u_i^2\}.
\]
When \(0\notin[\ell_i^2,u_i^2]\) for every \(i\), define
\[
B_1/B_2=\prod_{i=1}^n[\min Q_i,\max Q_i],\quad Q_i=\{\ell_i^1/\ell_i^2,\ell_i^1/u_i^2,u_i^1/\ell_i^2,u_i^1/u_i^2\}.
\]
Addition and multiplication are commutative and associative, whereas difference and division are not generally inverse operations. Moreover,
\[
B_1*(B_2+B_3)\subseteq B_1*B_2+B_1*B_3,
\]
and equality holds in special cases, including when \(B_1\) is a singleton box. The source states only \(\mathbf 0\notin B_2\) for division; for \(n>1\), that condition alone does not exclude zero from every denominator coordinate interval and therefore does not by itself make all displayed quotients well-defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Box arithmetic is defined coordinatewise using endpoint formulas. Addition and multiplication are commutative and associative, but subtraction and division do not generally provide inverse cancellation, and multiplication is only subdistributive over addition. The displayed division formula requires every denominator coordinate interval to exclude zero; the source's weaker condition that the zero vector not belong to the denominator box is insufficient in dimensions greater than one.
assumptions_latex: B_j=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i^j,u_i^j],\quad j=1,2
0\notin[\ell_i^2,u_i^2]\quad\text{for every }i\text{ when division is used}
B_1,B_2,B_3\in\mathcal B_n\quad\text{for the algebraic properties}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B_1*(B_2+B_3)\subseteq B_1*B_2+B_1*B_3;\quad\text{addition and multiplication are commutative and associative, while distributivity and inverse cancellation fail in general.}

children.title: Inclusion Isotonicity
children.top_down_role: Order-preserving behavior of interval mappings under nested input sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Inclusion Isotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States monotonicity of an interval extension with respect to set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(F\) map admissible interval boxes in \(D\) to interval boxes in \(\mathbb{R}^m\). The interval extension \(F\) is inclusion isotonic if, for every pair of admissible boxes \(X,Y\),
\[
X\subseteq Y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F(X)\subseteq F(Y).
\]
Thus enlarging the input box cannot shrink the computed image enclosure. This order property is distinct from range containment: inclusion isotonicity alone does not imply \(f(X)\subseteq F(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interval extension is inclusion isotonic when nested input boxes always produce correspondingly nested output boxes; this does not alone guarantee containment of the true range.
assumptions_latex: \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is defined on \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(F\) is defined on a family of interval boxes contained in \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\subseteq Y\) implies \(F(X)\subseteq F(Y)\) for all admissible boxes \(X,Y\).

notation.meaning: pointwise image set of X under f

children.title: Validated Range Containment

knowledge_statements.title: Validated Range Containment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes an interval result as a certificate enclosing every attainable function value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(X\subseteq D\) be an interval box. An interval result \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a validated range-containment certificate for \(f\) on \(X\) when
\[
f(X):=\{f(x):x\in X\}\subseteq Y.
\]
Equivalently, every \(x\in X\) satisfies \(f(x)\in Y\). If \(Y=F(X)\) is produced by an interval evaluator whose primitive operations are valid enclosures and whose expression composition preserves inclusion, then \(F(X)\) supplies this certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validated interval result certifies that every function value attained on the input box lies inside the reported output box.
assumptions_latex: \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(X\subseteq D\).
Every primitive interval operation used by \(F\) encloses its corresponding real operation.
Composition in \(F\) preserves the primitive containment guarantees.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq F(X)\), so \(F(X)\) is a range-containment certificate.

notation.meaning: exact pointwise range of f over X

children.title: Containment Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Containment Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when interval evaluation ceases to certify the real range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The implication \(f(X)\subseteq F(X)\) is not guaranteed if any primitive result fails to contain its exact real image, if an intermediate real operation is undefined, or if the implemented expression differs from \(f\). Concretely, let \(X=[1,2]\) and let an invalid squaring evaluator return \(Q(X)=[1,3]\). Since
\[
\{x^2:x\in X\}=[1,4]\nsubseteq[1,3],
\]
range containment already fails at that primitive. Any enclosing computation that uses \(Q(X)\) without independent correction therefore loses its validation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Containment can fail through inward rounding, invalid primitive domains, or expression mismatch; one missed attainable value invalidates all certificates depending on that enclosure.
assumptions_latex: The implemented squaring operation returns \(Q(X)=[1,3]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The attainable value \(4\) is absent from \(Q(X)\), so \(\{x^2:x\in X\}\nsubseteq Q(X)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Downward Directed Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the representable lower rounding used for outward interval endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb{F}\subset
eqq\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be an ordered floating-point set containing the supported infinities. For an exact real or extended-real result \(r\), downward directed rounding is
\[
\operatorname{rd}_{\downarrow}(r):=\max\{f\in\mathbb{F}:f\le r\},
\]
whenever the maximum exists under the format's overflow convention. It satisfies \(\operatorname{rd}_{\downarrow}(r)\le r\) and is the greatest representable value with that property. Applied to an exact lower endpoint, it therefore cannot move the endpoint inward.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Downward directed rounding returns the greatest representable number no larger than the exact result, making it suitable for validated lower endpoints.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb{F}\) is an ordered floating-point set with a specified overflow convention.
The set \(\{f\in\mathbb{F}:f\le r\}\) has a maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rd}_{\downarrow}(r)\le r\), with no larger member of \(\mathbb{F}\) satisfying this inequality.

children.title: Upward Directed Rounding
children.top_down_role: Upper-endpoint evaluation under containment-preserving finite-precision rounding.

knowledge_statements.title: Upward Directed Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the representable upper rounding used for outward interval endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb{F}\subset
eqq\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be an ordered floating-point set containing the supported infinities. For an exact real or extended-real result \(r\), upward directed rounding is
\[
\operatorname{rd}_{\uparrow}(r):=\min\{f\in\mathbb{F}:f\ge r\},
\]
whenever the minimum exists under the format's overflow convention. It satisfies \(r\le\operatorname{rd}_{\uparrow}(r)\) and is the least representable value with that property. Applied to an exact upper endpoint, it therefore cannot move the endpoint inward.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upward directed rounding returns the least representable number no smaller than the exact result, making it suitable for validated upper endpoints.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb{F}\) is an ordered floating-point set with a specified overflow convention.
The set \(\{f\in\mathbb{F}:f\ge r\}\) has a minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\le\operatorname{rd}_{\uparrow}(r)\), with no smaller member of \(\mathbb{F}\) satisfying this inequality.

children.title: Outward-Enclosure Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Containment guarantees obtained from paired endpoint rounding.

knowledge_statements.title: Outward-Enclosure Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States how directed endpoint rounding preserves containment of exact interval results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose an exact real operation over interval inputs has image hull \([L,U]\), where \(L,U\in\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) and \(L\le U\). If the implemented result is
\[
\widehat{Z}:=[\operatorname{rd}_{\downarrow}(L),\operatorname{rd}_{\uparrow}(U)],
\]
then
\[
[L,U]\subseteq\widehat{Z}.
\]
More generally, a finite expression evaluated by primitive interval operations with outward-rounded lower and upper bounds retains range containment, provided every intermediate operation uses valid domain semantics and each primitive exact image is bounded by the endpoints being rounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rounding exact lower bounds downward and exact upper bounds upward produces an interval containing the exact image; valid composition preserves this guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \([L,U]\) is the exact image hull of the real operation.
Directed rounding satisfies \(\operatorname{rd}_{\downarrow}(L)\le L\) and \(U\le\operatorname{rd}_{\uparrow}(U)\).
All composed primitives use valid domains and enclosing endpoint formulas.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([L,U]\subseteq[\operatorname{rd}_{\downarrow}(L),\operatorname{rd}_{\uparrow}(U)]\).

children.title: Rounding-Mode Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of containment caused by unsupported operations, mode leakage, or platform behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Rounding-Mode Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why uncontrolled or inward endpoint rounding destroys validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_-<f_+\) be adjacent representable numbers and let an exact endpoint \(r\) satisfy \(f_-<r<f_+\). If \(r\) is a lower bound but is rounded to \(f_+\), then values in \([r,f_+)\) are excluded. If \(r\) is an upper bound but is rounded to \(f_-\), then values in \((f_-,r]\) are excluded. Hence round-to-nearest, truncation, compiler reassociation, or an unverified rounding mode cannot by itself certify outward containment; each lower endpoint must be no greater, and each upper endpoint no smaller, than its exact counterpart.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any lower endpoint rounded upward or upper endpoint rounded downward can omit attainable values. Uncontrolled rounding modes therefore cannot establish a validated enclosure.
assumptions_latex: \(f_-<f_+\) are adjacent values in the working floating-point format.
The exact endpoint \(r\) lies strictly between them.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Choosing \(f_+\) as a lower bound or \(f_-\) as an upper bound yields an inward, non-enclosing endpoint.

children.title: Exceptional-Domain Interval Systems
children.top_down_role: Representations for unbounded results, exceptional operations, and domain-status tracking.

children.title: Extended Interval Systems
children.top_down_role: Interval representations accommodating unbounded endpoints and extended results.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended Interval Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines intervals with infinite endpoints and explicit empty-set support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}:=\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}\). An extended interval system is
\[
\overline{\mathbb{IR}}:=\{\varnothing\}\cup\{[a,b]:a,b\in\overline{\mathbb{R}},\ a\le b\},
\]
where \([a,b]\) denotes \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}:a\le x\le b\}\) with the usual extended-order interpretation. Thus \([{-\infty},b]\), \([a,+\infty]\), and \([{-\infty},+\infty]\) represent unbounded real sets, while \(\varnothing\) represents no feasible value. Arithmetic must separately specify results for undefined or discontinuous operations; membership in this carrier alone does not determine those exceptional semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended interval system adds infinite endpoints and the empty interval to bounded real intervals, while leaving exceptional-operation behavior to a separately specified arithmetic semantics.
assumptions_latex: \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) carries the standard total order extending the real order.
Intervals denote subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\), not sets containing infinity as an attainable real value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\mathbb{IR}}\) contains bounded, one-sided unbounded, entire, and empty real interval sets.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An authoritative source with a specific locator is required. Extended interval carriers vary over whether singleton infinities, the empty interval, and exceptional-operation semantics are included; as written, allowing a=b=+infinity or a=b=-infinity while interpreting intervals as subsets of the real numbers also duplicates the empty set. Source alignment is needed before selecting and correcting the intended variant.

children.title: Decorated Interval Systems
children.top_down_role: Interval representations carrying validity or domain-quality metadata.

knowledge_statements.title: Decorated Interval Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: IEEE-style real decorated intervals with five ordered domain-quality decorations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decorated interval is a pair \(\boldsymbol{x}=(X,d)\), where \(X\) is a closed real interval, possibly empty or unbounded, and \(d\in\{\mathrm{ill},\mathrm{trv},\mathrm{def},\mathrm{dac},\mathrm{com}\}\), ordered by \(\mathrm{ill}<\mathrm{trv}<\mathrm{def}<\mathrm{dac}<\mathrm{com}\). The decoration records progressively stronger information about whether the represented computation is defined, continuous, and bounded on its input box. The empty ill-formed object is \((\varnothing,\mathrm{ill})\); every nonempty valid decorated interval has decoration at least \(\mathrm{trv}\). A decorated operation returns an enclosing interval together with a decoration no stronger than either its input decorations or its operation-specific domain guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decorated interval couples an interval enclosure with an ordered tag recording the computation’s definedness, continuity, and boundedness guarantees.
assumptions_latex: The underlying arithmetic uses closed real intervals, allowing empty and unbounded intervals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\boldsymbol{x}=(X,d)\) carries both a set enclosure \(X\) and a domain-quality guarantee \(d\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition broadly matches decorated interval arithmetic, but the exact admissible interval-decoration pairs and operation-propagation rule are standard-specific and have no citation.

children.title: Exceptional-Operation Semantics
children.top_down_role: Representation outcomes for undefined, discontinuous, or partially defined operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Exceptional-Operation Semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-based semantics for interval extensions of partial real operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be a partial real operation and let \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_n\) be an interval box. Its exceptional-domain interval evaluation is \[G(X)=\operatorname{hull}\{g(x):x\in X\cap D\}.\] If \(X\cap D=\varnothing\), the result is empty and marked ill-formed; if \(X\not\subseteq D\) but \(X\cap D\neq\varnothing\), the defined values remain enclosed while the status is weakened to record the domain violation. Thus undefined point operations do not authorize discarding any defined values or returning an unenclosed finite substitute.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial operation encloses all values at defined points of the box, returning empty only when no point lies in its domain.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is interpreted as a partial real-valued operation with domain \(D\).
The hull is taken in the chosen extended interval system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(X\cap D)\subseteq G(X)\), with status distinguishing empty, partial-domain, and full-domain evaluation.

notation.meaning: Real domain of the partial operation.
Exceptional-domain interval extension of the operation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-based enclosure is plausible, but marking an empty result from an empty domain intersection as ill-formed is convention-sensitive and conflicts with standards in which ill is reserved for NaI while an empty computed interval receives a weaker non-ill decoration.

children.title: Domain-Status Propagation
children.top_down_role: Preservation of domain and validity status through composite interval evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Status Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional propagation of decorated domain information through an expression tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an expression tree, assign each leaf its interval \(X_i\) and input decoration \(d_i\). At an internal node representing a partial operation \(g\), compute the set enclosure \(Y=G(X_1,\ldots,X_k)\) and its local domain decoration \(d_g\). Return \[(Y,d)=\bigl(Y,\min\{d_g,d_1,\ldots,d_k\}\bigr)\] in the decoration order. Process nodes from leaves to root. Stop with \((\varnothing,\mathrm{ill})\) when an internal operation has no defined argument tuple; otherwise output the root enclosure and its propagated decoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate bottom-up, enclosing defined values and assigning each node the weakest of its input statuses and local domain guarantee.
assumptions_latex: Every elementary operation supplies an inclusion function and a local domain-status rule.
Decoration order is \(\mathrm{ill}<\mathrm{trv}<\mathrm{def}<\mathrm{dac}<\mathrm{com}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The root interval encloses every defined real evaluation, and its decoration cannot exceed any status encountered along the expression tree.

notation.meaning: Local decoration produced by an operation’s domain rule.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bottom-up minimum rule resembles decorated propagation, but operation-specific decoration semantics must be sourced. In particular, returning ill whenever no defined tuple exists is not reliable without a specified standard.

children.title: Natural Interval Extensions
children.top_down_role: Expression-based interval evaluation using elementary inclusion functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Natural Interval Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Natural inclusion function obtained by interval evaluation of a fixed real expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an expression \(e\) represent \(f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), and suppose every constant and elementary operation in \(e\) has an inclusion-isotonic interval extension. The natural interval extension \(F_e\) is obtained by replacing each variable \(x_i\) by \(X_i\) and evaluating the unchanged expression with those interval operations. For every interval box \(X\subseteq D\), \[f(X)=\{f(x):x\in X\}\subseteq F_e(X).\] Different algebraically equivalent expressions may therefore produce different enclosures because repeated occurrences of a variable are evaluated as independent interval operands.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace every operation in a real expression by its interval counterpart; the result encloses the expression’s range but depends on its syntax.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq D\) is an interval box.
Each elementary interval operation encloses its corresponding real operation and is inclusion isotonic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq F_e(X)\).

notation.meaning: Fixed expression representing the real function.
Natural interval extension determined by that expression.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Natural Interval Extension of an Explicit Expression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to a fixed explicit expression formed without logical or conditional control constructs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\), be represented by a fixed expression using variables, real constants, the four arithmetic operations, and predeclared functions, without logical or conditional statements. For \(Y\in\mathbf I(D)\), its natural interval extension is obtained by replacing every occurrence of the variables by \(Y\), each real arithmetic operation by its interval counterpart, and each predeclared function \(g\) by a corresponding inclusion function \(G\). The notation \(f(Y)\) denotes both the resulting interval expression and its evaluated value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed explicit expression without conditional control flow, replace variables by an interval box, real arithmetic by interval arithmetic, and predeclared functions by corresponding inclusion functions. The resulting expression and its evaluated interval are denoted by f(Y).
assumptions_latex: D\subseteq\mathbb R^m
f:D\to\mathbb R
Y\in\mathbf I(D)
f\text{ has a fixed expression using variables, constants, arithmetic operations, and predeclared functions without logical or conditional statements}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(Y)\text{ is obtained by the substitutions }x\mapsto Y,\;*_{\mathbb R}\mapsto *_{\mathbf I},\;g\mapsto G

children.title: Centered First-Order Enclosure Family
children.top_down_role: First-order enclosures organized around a selected center.

children.title: Centered Forms
children.top_down_role: Center-based inclusion forms using localized representations over a box.

knowledge_statements.title: Centered Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order enclosure built from a center and interval coefficient functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a box, choose \(c\in X\), and suppose interval functions \(A_i(X,c)\) satisfy \[f(x)-f(c)\in\sum_{i=1}^n A_i(X,c)(x_i-c_i)\qquad(x\in X).\] The associated centered form is \[F_c(X)=f(c)+\sum_{i=1}^n A_i(X,c)(X_i-c_i).\] It is an inclusion function because every pointwise increment is contained in the corresponding interval sum. The coefficients may arise from derivatives, slopes, or an algebraically centered expression; their construction determines the enclosure’s sharpness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A centered form encloses function increments from a chosen center using interval coefficients multiplying coordinate deviations.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is finite at the chosen center \(c\in X\).
The coefficient intervals satisfy the displayed pointwise increment inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq F_c(X)\).

notation.meaning: Chosen center in the interval box.
Interval coefficient for the ith coordinate increment.

children.title: Mean-Value Forms
children.top_down_role: First-order range enclosures combining center values with derivative ranges.

knowledge_statements.title: Mean-Value Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar multivariate first-order mean-value enclosure on a convex interval box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a convex interval box, let \(c\in X\), and let \(f\) be continuously differentiable on an open set containing \(X\). If \(G_i(X)\) encloses \(\partial_i f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) and every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), then the mean-value form \[M_c(X)=f(c)+\sum_{i=1}^n G_i(X)(X_i-c_i)\] satisfies \[f(X)\subseteq M_c(X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable scalar function, derivative bounds over a convex box multiplied by deviations from a center give a rigorous enclosure of the function's range.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a convex interval box and \(c\in X\).
\(f\) is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(X\).
For every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(x\in X\), \(\partial_i f(x)\in G_i(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq f(c)+\sum_{i=1}^nG_i(X)(X_i-c_i)\).

notation.meaning: Interval enclosure of the ith partial derivative over the box.
Mean-value interval form centered at c.

children.title: Center Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Midpoint, interior-point, incumbent-based, and adaptive center choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Center Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissibility and common deterministic choices for centers in first-order forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a centered or mean-value form on \(X=\prod_{i=1}^n[\underline x_i,\overline x_i]\), an admissible center satisfies \(c\in X\). Three standard regimes are: the midpoint center \(c_i=(\underline x_i+\overline x_i)/2\) for bounded coordinates; an incumbent or sampled center \(c\in X\) when a useful feasible point is known; and a fixed endpoint center with \(c_i\in\{\underline x_i,\overline x_i\}\). Any regime preserves inclusion when the underlying increment representation is valid, although enclosure width and numerical stability can differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any center inside the box preserves validity; midpoint, feasible-point, and endpoint choices produce different enclosure widths and numerical behavior.
assumptions_latex: The first-order increment representation is valid for every point of \(X\).
A midpoint regime is used only for coordinates with finite endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every selected \(c\in X\) yields a valid centered enclosure, but validity alone does not determine the sharpest center.

notation.meaning: Center selected for the first-order enclosure.
Lower and upper endpoints of coordinate interval i.

children.title: Center-Dependent Overestimation
children.top_down_role: Enclosure degradation associated with unsuitable or unstable center choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Center-Dependent Overestimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A computable dependence bound for mean-value enclosure radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write \(X_i=[m_i-r_i,m_i+r_i]\) and \(G_i=[a_i-s_i,a_i+s_i]\), with \(r_i,s_i\geq0\). For any \(c\in X\), the mean-value form obeys \[\operatorname{rad} M_c(X)\leq\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(|a_i|r_i+s_i|m_i-c_i|+s_i r_i\bigr).\] Hence the center-dependent part of this standard interval-product bound is \(\sum_i s_i|m_i-c_i|\), which is minimized by the midpoint center \(c=m\). This bound need not identify the center producing the exact narrowest enclosure because \(f(c)\) and dependency effects may also vary with \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A center’s displacement from the box midpoint increases a standard radius bound in proportion to derivative-interval uncertainty.
assumptions_latex: \(M_c(X)=f(c)+\sum_iG_i(X)(X_i-c_i)\) is evaluated with ordinary interval operations.
All coordinate and derivative intervals are bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed radius bound is minimized over \(c\in X\) at \(c=m\).

notation.meaning: Midpoint and radius of coordinate interval i.
Midpoint and radius of derivative interval i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed interval-product radius bound is mathematically plausible and the midpoint minimizes its center-dependent term, but this nontrivial explicit bound has no cited evidence.

children.title: Slope Forms
children.top_down_role: Finite-region slope representations used in validated range computation.

knowledge_statements.title: Slope Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Point-centered interval representation using generalized secant coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\), choose \(c\in X\), and suppose a slope vector \(s(x,c)\) is defined so that \[f(x)-f(c)=s(x,c)^{\mathsf T}(x-c)\qquad(x\in X).\] If interval coefficients \(S_i(X,c)\) enclose every component \(s_i(x,c)\), then the slope form \[F_s(X)=f(c)+\sum_{i=1}^n S_i(X,c)(X_i-c_i)\] encloses \(f(X)\). Unlike a derivative form, this representation requires an exact secant identity and interval bounds on slopes, not differentiability throughout \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enclose exact secant coefficients from a center, then multiply them by coordinate deviations to obtain a rigorous range enclosure.
assumptions_latex: \(f(c)\) is finite and the displayed slope identity holds throughout \(X\).
\(s_i(x,c)\in S_i(X,c)\) for all \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq F_s(X)\).

notation.meaning: Pointwise slope vector joining c to x.
Interval enclosure of the ith slope component.

children.title: Divided-Difference Forms
children.top_down_role: Enclosures based on divided differences across selected points or regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Divided-Difference Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Telescoping coordinatewise representation of a multivariate function increment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,c\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define \(z^0=c\) and \(z^i=(x_1,\ldots,x_i,c_{i+1},\ldots,c_n)\). When \(x_i\neq c_i\), define \[q_i(x,c)=\frac{f(z^i)-f(z^{i-1})}{x_i-c_i};\] when \(x_i=c_i\), choose any real value for \(q_i(x,c)\). Then \[f(x)=f(c)+\sum_{i=1}^n q_i(x,c)(x_i-c_i).\] If \(Q_i(X,c)\) encloses every selected \(q_i(x,c)\) for \(x\in X\), then \[f(X)\subseteq f(c)+\sum_{i=1}^nQ_i(X,c)(X_i-c_i).\] The representation can depend on the chosen coordinate order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinatewise telescoping path from the center expresses each function increment using divided differences; interval enclosures of the selected coefficients yield a range enclosure.
assumptions_latex: For every \(x\in X\), each intermediate point \(z^i\) belongs to the domain of \(f\).
For every \(i\), \(Q_i(X,c)\) encloses all selected values \(q_i(x,c)\) with \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq f(c)+\sum_{i=1}^nQ_i(X,c)(X_i-c_i)\).

notation.meaning: Intermediate point after replacing the first i center coordinates.
Coordinatewise divided difference, with an arbitrary selected value on a zero coordinate increment.
Interval enclosure of the selected divided differences.

children.title: Nonsmooth Representation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Use of finite-region representations where point derivatives are unavailable or weak.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Representation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slope identities can survive nondifferentiability, whereas derivative mean-value forms cannot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=|x|\) and center \(c=0\), the exact identity \[f(x)-f(0)=s(x,0)x\] holds with \(s(x,0)=1\) for \(x>0\), \(s(x,0)=-1\) for \(x<0\), and any \(s(0,0)\in[-1,1]\). Thus, on every interval \(X\) containing zero, \(S(X,0)=[-1,1]\) yields the valid slope enclosure \(|X|\subseteq[-1,1]X\). A classical mean-value form requiring continuous differentiability on a neighborhood of \(X\) is unavailable because \(|x|\) is not differentiable at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For absolute value across zero, bounded secant slopes give a valid enclosure although the classical differentiable mean-value hypothesis fails.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R\) is an interval containing \(0\).
Slope values at the diagonal are selected from \([-1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A slope form remains valid on \(X\), while the classical continuously differentiable mean-value theorem does not apply.

notation.meaning: Interval enclosure of slopes from the center zero.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The absolute-value example correctly illustrates that an exact slope representation can remain available where the classical continuously differentiable mean-value theorem does not apply, but the record supplies no source.

children.title: Newton-Operator Integration
children.top_down_role: Use of slope-based representations within validated local contraction operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Newton-Operator Integration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval Newton contraction using a slope-matrix enclosure instead of a derivative enclosure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), a box \(X\), and \(c\in X\), construct an interval matrix \(S(X,c)\) such that \[F(x)-F(c)=S(x,c)(x-c),\qquad S(x,c)\in S(X,c),\] for every \(x\in X\). Compute an interval enclosure \(Y\) of all solutions of the interval linear system \[S(X,c)y=-F(c),\] and set \(X^+=X\cap(c+Y)\). If \(X^+=\varnothing\), certify that \(X\) contains no zero; otherwise continue with \(X^+\), stopping when contraction or width tolerances are met and returning the final enclosing box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insert an interval slope matrix into the interval Newton equation, intersect its solution enclosure with the current box, and iterate.
assumptions_latex: The slope identity holds for every \(x\in X\).
The interval linear solver encloses every solution generated by point matrices in \(S(X,c)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every zero of \(F\) in \(X\) lies in \(X^+\); hence \(X^+=\varnothing\) excludes zeros from \(X\).

notation.meaning: Interval enclosure of slope matrices about c.
Enclosure of corrections solving the interval linear system.

children.title: Interval Taylor Forms
children.top_down_role: Higher-order local enclosures with validated remainder ranges.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\prod_{i=1}^n[\underline x_i,\overline x_i]\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(c\in X\).
\(f\) is \(p\)-times continuously differentiable on an open convex neighborhood of \(X\), where \(p\ge 1\).
Each interval \([D^\alpha f](X)\) encloses \(\{D^\alpha f(x):x\in X\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq T_p(f,X,c)\).

notation.meaning: The order-p interval Taylor form about c.

review_flags: locator_supports_interval-method context but exact Taylor formula requires source confirmation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multivariate order-\(p\) Taylor enclosure with interval-valued highest-order remainder.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in X\), define the interval Taylor form
\[
T_p(f,X,c)=\sum_{|\alpha|<p}\frac{D^\alpha f(c)}{\alpha!}(X-c)^\alpha+\sum_{|\alpha|=p}\frac{[D^\alpha f](X)}{\alpha!}(X-c)^\alpha.
\]
All sums and products in this expression use inclusion-isotone interval arithmetic. The multivariate Taylor formula with remainder implies
\[
\{f(x):x\in X\}\subseteq T_p(f,X,c).
\]
Thus the displayed interval is a validated range enclosure; its highest-order coefficients range over all derivative values on \(X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Interval Taylor Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the quadratic Taylor inclusion form and the associated boundedness condition for its Hessian enclosure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:D\to\mathbb R$, $D\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, be twice differentiable, and let $F'':\mathbf I(D)\to\mathbf I^{m\times m}$ be an inclusion function for $f''$. For $Y\in\mathbf I(D)$ and $c\in Y$, define
$$T_2(Y)=f(c)+(Y-c)^T f'(c)+\frac12 (Y-c)^T F''(Y)(Y-c).$$
Then $T_2$ is an inclusion function for $f$. The inclusion function $F''$ is bounded if there exists $C\in\mathbf I^{m\times m}$ such that $F''(Y)\subseteq C$ for every $Y\in\mathbf I(D)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second-order interval Taylor form combines the function value and gradient at an expansion point with an interval Hessian enclosure and contains the function range on the box. The Hessian enclosure is bounded when one interval matrix contains its values on all admissible boxes.
assumptions_latex: f:D\to\mathbb R,\quad D\subseteq\mathbb R^m
f\text{ is twice differentiable}
Y\in\mathbf I(D),\quad c\in Y
F''\text{ is an inclusion function for }f''
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in Y,\quad f(x)\in T_2(Y),\qquad F''\text{ bounded}\iff \exists C\in\mathbf I^{m\times m}\ \forall Y\in\mathbf I(D),\ F''(Y)\subseteq C

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\{\nabla f(x):x\in X\}\subseteq[\nabla f](X).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Convexity from an Interval Hessian Enclosure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient interval-matrix test for uniform convexity on a compact interval box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuously twice differentiable on a compact interval box \(X\), and let \(H\) be a symmetric interval matrix satisfying \(\nabla^2f(x)\in H\) componentwise for every \(x\in X\). If \(H\) contains a symmetric positive-definite matrix \(H_0\) and every symmetric matrix belonging to \(H\) is nonsingular, then every symmetric matrix in \(H\) is positive definite. Consequently, \(f\) is uniformly convex on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a symmetric interval matrix encloses every Hessian on a compact box, contains one positive-definite symmetric matrix, and contains no singular symmetric matrix, then all its symmetric matrices are positive definite. The function is therefore uniformly convex on the box.

\exists H_0\in H:\ H_0=H_0^\top\text{ and }H_0\succ0.
\forall A\in H,\ A=A^\top\Longrightarrow A\text{ is nonsingular.}

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Hessian Spectral Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gershgorin certificate for eigenvalues of every Hessian in an interval matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex box, let \(f\) be twice continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(X\), and let \(\mathcal H=([h_{ij}])_{i,j=1}^n\) be a symmetric interval matrix satisfying \(\nabla^2 f(x)\in\mathcal H\) for every \(x\in X\). Set \(r_i=\sum_{j\ne i}\operatorname{mag}([h_{ij}])\), where \(\operatorname{mag}([a,b])=\max\{|a|,|b|\}\), and define
\[
\lambda_G^- =\min_{1\le i\le n}\{\inf[h_{ii}]-r_i\},\qquad
\lambda_G^+ =\max_{1\le i\le n}\{\sup[h_{ii}]+r_i\}.
\]
For every \(H\in\mathcal H\), Gershgorin's theorem gives
\[
\sigma(H)\subseteq[\lambda_G^-,\lambda_G^+].
\]
Consequently, \(\lambda_G^->0\) certifies that \(f\) is strictly convex on \(X\), while \(\lambda_G^+<0\) certifies that \(f\) is strictly concave on \(X\). If neither inequality holds, this certificate is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gershgorin bounds computed from an interval Hessian enclose every eigenvalue of every represented Hessian; a positive lower bound certifies strict convexity, and a negative upper bound certifies strict concavity on the convex box.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty convex box.
\(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(X\).
\(\mathcal H=([h_{ij}])_{i,j=1}^n\) is a symmetric interval matrix and \(\nabla^2f(x)\in\mathcal H\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(H\in\mathcal H\), \(\sigma(H)\subseteq[\lambda_G^-,\lambda_G^+]\); moreover, \(\lambda_G^->0\) certifies strict convexity and \(\lambda_G^+<0\) certifies strict concavity on \(X\).

notation.meaning: The symmetric interval matrix enclosing every Hessian on X.
The maximum absolute magnitude of an interval.
The set of eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix H.

\]
Return the intervals at output nodes as value enclosures and their propagated gradients as rows of an interval Jacobian. The stopping convention is completion of the finite graph; outward rounding makes every returned value and derivative enclosure validated.

children.title: Dependency Overestimation
children.top_down_role: Loss of dependence information under componentwise interval evaluation.

assumptions_latex: The expression \(f(x)=x-x\) is evaluated by the natural interval extension, treating repeated occurrences independently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The natural interval extension strictly overestimates the exact range by width \(2(b-a)\).

notation.meaning: Natural interval evaluation of the displayed expression.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical repeated-variable counterexample for componentwise interval evaluation.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The exact range is
\[
f(X)=\{x-x:x\in X\}=\{0\}.
\]
Natural interval evaluation loses the equality between the two occurrences of \(x\) and gives
\[
F_N(X)=X-X=[a-b,b-a].
\]
Therefore \(f(X)\subsetneq F_N(X)\) and
\[
\operatorname{wid}(F_N(X))=2(b-a)>0=\operatorname{wid}(f(X)).
\]
The excess arises solely from discarded dependence information; algebraically simplifying the expression to the constant zero removes it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Although x minus itself is identically zero, independent interval evaluation of its repeated occurrences returns a nonzero interval, exhibiting dependency overestimation.

children.top_down_role: Width growth caused by repeated enclosure of transformed regions.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is planar rotation through angle \(\pi/4\).
\(B_0=[-1,1]^2\), and \(B_{k+1}=\operatorname{box}(QB_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeated axis-aligned reenclosure expands box radius as \(2^{k/2}\) although the exact rotated set remains bounded.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(r>0\), the axis-aligned hull of \(Q[-r,r]^2\) is \([-\sqrt2r,\sqrt2r]^2\). Consequently the recurrence gives
\[
B_k=[-2^{k/2},2^{k/2}]^2.
\]
In contrast, the exact propagated set after \(k\) steps is \(Q^kB_0\), which is merely a rotation of \(B_0\) and has constant Euclidean diameter \(2\sqrt2\). Thus replacing each rotated set by its axis-aligned box destroys orientation information and causes unbounded enclosure growth despite bounded exact dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly boxing a rotated square enlarges its enclosure by a factor of square-root two per step, while the exact rotated square keeps constant diameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-Enclosure Accumulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies wrapping growth caused by repeatedly replacing transformed sets with axis-aligned interval hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{2\times2}\) be rotation through an angle \(\theta\) with \(0<\theta<\pi/2\), and let \(X_0=[-1,1]^2\). Define \(X_{k+1}=\operatorname{hull}_{\Box}(A X_k)\), where \(\operatorname{hull}_{\Box}\) is the smallest axis-aligned box containing its argument. Then \(X_k=[-s_k,s_k]^2\), with \(s_k=(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)^k\). Although \(A^kX_0\) has constant area, \(\operatorname{area}(X_k)=4(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)^{2k}\), so repeated reenclosure accumulates exponentially growing overestimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated axis-aligned enclosure of a rotated square can grow exponentially even though exact rotations preserve its area.

knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate-Quantity Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents an expression by auxiliary variables while preserving its real graph but changing interval propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let an expression for \(f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be represented by a directed acyclic evaluation graph with intermediate operations \(z_j=\phi_j(z_{p(j)})\). Introduce one variable \(z_j\) and one equality for every internal node. Then
\[\{(x,y):x\in D,\ y=f(x)\}=\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}\{(x,z,y):x\in D,\ z_j=\phi_j(z_{p(j)}),\ y=z_m\}.\]
Algebraically equivalent graphs therefore define the same real input-output relation, but their interval evaluations or contractor propagation may differ because variable occurrences and intermediate domains differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary variables preserve an expression's exact real graph, yet different evaluation graphs can produce different interval enclosures and propagation strength.
assumptions_latex: The evaluation graph is finite and acyclic.
Every intermediate operation is defined on the values generated from \(D\).

children.title: Contracting Inclusion-Function Classes

children.title: Convergent Inclusion Functions
children.top_down_role: Inclusion-function families whose excess width vanishes under domain refinement.

knowledge_statements.title: Convergent Inclusion Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines pointwise convergence of an interval inclusion function on boxes shrinking around a point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f:D\to\mathbb R^m\), and let \(F\) map every box \(X\subseteq D\) to an interval box satisfying \(f(X)\subseteq F(X)\). The inclusion function \(F\) is convergent at \(x\in D\) if, for every sequence of boxes \((X_k)\) such that \(x\in X_k\subseteq D\) and \(\operatorname{diam}(X_k)\to0\), one has \(\operatorname{diam}(F(X_k))\to0\). It is convergent on \(D\) if it is convergent at every \(x\in D\). Since \(f(x)\in F(X_k)\), convergence also implies that \(F(X_k)\) converges to the singleton \(\{f(x)\}\) in Hausdorff distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergent inclusion function produces output boxes converging to the point value whenever input boxes containing that point shrink to it.
assumptions_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq F(X)\) for every admissible box \(X\).
Input and output diameters use fixed norms.
Every shrinking box in the pointwise condition contains \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in X_k\) and \(\operatorname{diam}(X_k)\to0\) imply \(\operatorname{diam}(F(X_k))\to0\) and \(F(X_k)\to\{f(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: Set or box diameter under a fixed norm.

children.title: Lipschitz Inclusion Functions
children.top_down_role: Inclusion-function families with width behavior controlled by box diameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Inclusion Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a linear output-diameter bound for an interval inclusion function using max-norm box diameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(X_0\subseteq D\) be a box, and let \(F\) be an inclusion function on all boxes contained in \(X_0\). Using the max norm in the input and output spaces, \(F\) is Lipschitz on \(X_0\) if there exists \(L_F<\infty\) such that, for every box \(X\subseteq X_0\), \[\operatorname{diam}_\infty(F(X))\le L_F\operatorname{diam}_\infty(X).\] This bound implies convergence of \(F\) on boxes shrinking around points of \(X_0\). Moreover, because \(f(X)\subseteq F(X)\), it implies \(\lVert f(x)-f(y)\rVert_\infty\le L_F\lVert x-y\rVert_\infty\) for all \(x,y\in X_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lipschitz inclusion function has max-norm output-box diameter bounded linearly by input-box diameter; it converges on shrinking boxes and bounds the Lipschitz constant of the enclosed function.
assumptions_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq F(X)\) for every box \(X\subseteq X_0\).
Input and output diameters are induced by their respective max norms.
\(F\) is defined on degenerate boxes and on the box hull of every pair of points in \(X_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{diam}_\infty(F(X))\le L_F\operatorname{diam}_\infty(X)\) for all boxes \(X\subseteq X_0\).

notation.meaning: Box on which the uniform diameter bound holds.
Diameter induced by the max norm.
