knowledge_statements.statement_title: Width-Lipschitz Interval Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines Lipschitz regularity for an interval-valued mapping through the widths of its input and output boxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) and \(F:\mathbf I(D)\to\mathbf I^k\). The interval mapping \(F\) is Lipschitz if there exists \(K\in\mathbb R\) such that \[w(F(Y))\le K\,w(Y)\qquad\text{for every }Y\in\mathbf I(D).\] This width property is independent of convergence order defined using excess width.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interval-valued mapping is width-Lipschitz when one constant bounds its output width by that constant times the input-box width for every admissible box. This property is independent of excess-width convergence order.
assumptions_latex: D\subseteq\mathbb R^m
F:\mathbf I(D)\to\mathbf I^k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists K\in\mathbb R\;\forall Y\in\mathbf I(D),\quad w(F(Y))\le K\,w(Y)

children.title: Excess-Width Decay Regimes
children.top_down_role: Qualitative rates and regularity regimes governing enclosure tightening.

knowledge_statements.title: Excess-Width Decay Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies enclosure sharpness by the asymptotic decay of width exceeding the exact range width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a scalar function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) and an interval inclusion function \(F\), define the excess width on a box \(X\subseteq D\) by
\[e_F(X)=\operatorname{wid}(F(X))-\operatorname{wid}(\operatorname{hull}(f(X)))\ge0.\]
For \(p>0\), \(F\) has excess-width decay of order \(p\) at \(x\in D\) if there exist \(C,\delta>0\) such that \(e_F(X)\le C\operatorname{diam}(X)^p\) for every box \(X\ni x\) with \(\operatorname{diam}(X)\le\delta\). Linear and quadratic regimes correspond respectively to \(p=1\) and \(p=2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Excess-width order measures how quickly an interval enclosure's width approaches the exact range-hull width on shrinking boxes.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) encloses \(f(X)\) for every admissible box \(X\).
The record concerns scalar-valued \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Order \(p\) means \(e_F(X)=O(\operatorname{diam}(X)^p)\) locally at \(x\).

notation.meaning: Enclosure width minus exact range-hull width.
Smallest real interval containing the exact range.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Excess Width and Convergence Order of an Inclusion Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines enclosure overestimation and its asymptotic decay with input-box width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be an inclusion function for \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), where \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\). Its excess width on \(Y\in\mathbf I(D)\) is \[w(F(Y))-w(\square f(Y)).\] For \(\alpha>0\), \(F\) has convergence order \(\alpha\) if \[w(F(Y))-w(\square f(Y))=\mathcal O\!\left(w(Y)^\alpha\right),\] namely, if there exists \(c\ge0\) such that \[w(F(Y))-w(\square f(Y))\le c\,w(Y)^\alpha\qquad\text{for every }Y\in\mathbf I(D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Excess width is the width of an inclusion enclosure minus the width of the exact range. An inclusion function has order alpha when this excess is bounded by a constant times the alpha-th power of the input-box width.
assumptions_latex: D\subseteq\mathbb R^m
f:D\to\mathbb R
F\text{ is an inclusion function for }f
\alpha>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists c\ge0\;\forall Y\in\mathbf I(D),\quad w(F(Y))-w(\square f(Y))\le c\,w(Y)^\alpha

children.title: Nonsmooth Convergence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Refinement behavior near discontinuities, singularities, or weakly regular regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Convergence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhibits loss of quadratic width decay at a nonsmooth point despite continued linear convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=|x|\) and let \(X_h=[-h,h]\) for \(h>0\). The natural interval evaluation gives \(F(X_h)=|X_h|=[0,h]\), so \(\operatorname{wid}(F(X_h))=h=\tfrac12\operatorname{diam}(X_h)\). Hence \(F(X_h)\to\{0\}\) linearly as \(h\downarrow0\), but no constant \(C\) can satisfy \(\operatorname{wid}(F(X_h))\le C\operatorname{diam}(X_h)^2\) for all sufficiently small \(h\). Nonsmoothness at zero therefore blocks a generally valid quadratic output-width bound, though it does not block convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For absolute value at its kink, natural interval width decays linearly, so convergence survives but a quadratic bound fails.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=|x|\) is evaluated naturally on \(X_h=[-h,h]\).
\(h>0\) tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{wid}(F(X_h))=\tfrac12\operatorname{diam}(X_h)\), which is not \(O(\operatorname{diam}(X_h)^2)\).

notation.meaning: Symmetric interval of radius h about the nonsmooth point.
Exact interval image of X_h under absolute value.

children.title: Contractor Algebra
children.top_down_role: Structural properties and compositions governing solution-preserving box contraction.

children.title: Contractor Solution Preservation
children.top_down_role: Containment discipline ensuring that contraction retains every target solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Contractor Solution Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the soundness condition requiring contraction to retain all feasible points in the input box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a target solution set. A solution-preserving contractor for \(S\) is a mapping \(C\) from boxes to boxes such that, for every box \(X\),
\[C(X)\subseteq X\qquad\text{and}\qquad X\cap S\subseteq C(X).\]
Equivalently, \(C\) may delete points only from \(X\setminus S\). If \(C(X)=\varnothing\), then the preservation condition certifies \(X\cap S=\varnothing\); if \(C(X)\ne\varnothing\), it makes no assertion that retained points are solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sound contractor shrinks a box without removing any target solution; an empty contracted box certifies infeasibility of the original box.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is fixed.
Contractor inputs and outputs are axis-aligned boxes, allowing the empty box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\cap S\subseteq C(X)\subseteq X\) for every input box \(X\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated contractor soundness condition and empty-box consequence are standard and internally correct, but no source is supplied for this nontrivial definition.

children.title: Contractor Composition
children.top_down_role: Sequential, parallel, and combined use of heterogeneous contractors.

knowledge_statements.title: Contractor Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States closure of solution preservation under sequential composition and box intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) be solution-preserving contractors for the same set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). Their sequential composition \(C_{\mathrm{seq}}=C_m\circ\cdots\circ C_1\) is solution-preserving. Their parallel intersection
\[C_{\cap}(X)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i(X)\]
is also solution-preserving whenever the intersection is represented as a box. Specifically, for every box \(X\), both constructions satisfy \(X\cap S\subseteq C_{\mathrm{seq}}(X)\subseteq X\) and \(X\cap S\subseteq C_{\cap}(X)\subseteq X\). Thus heterogeneous sound contractors can be combined without losing solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequentially applying sound contractors or intersecting their outputs remains sound for their common solution set.
assumptions_latex: Every \(C_i\) preserves the same solution set \(S\).
Each \(C_i(X)\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both \(C_m\circ\cdots\circ C_1\) and \(X\mapsto\bigcap_i C_i(X)\) preserve \(X\cap S\).

notation.meaning: Contractor formed by intersecting individual outputs.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Sequential composition and intersection preserve the common solution set under the stated contractor conditions, but the contractor-algebra property has no cited evidence.

children.title: Contractor Fixed-Point Closures
children.top_down_role: Repeated propagation toward stable contracted domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Contractor Fixed-Point Closures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterates a finite contractor family until no contractor produces further box reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an initial box \(X^{(0)}\), solution-preserving contractors \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\), and a fair index sequence \((i_k)\), compute
\[X^{(k+1)}=C_{i_k}(X^{(k)}).\]
Stop with the empty box if some \(X^{(k)}=\varnothing\). Otherwise stop when \(C_i(X^{(k)})=X^{(k)}\) for every \(i\), and output \(X^{(k)}\); under finite-precision arithmetic, equality means no representable bound changes. Every iterate contains \(X^{(0)}\cap S\). If the process terminates nonemptily, its output is a common fixed point of all scheduled contractors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly apply sound contractors fairly until none changes the box; every iterate preserves solutions and the result is a common fixed point.
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\) preserves the common solution set \(S\).
The schedule is fair: every contractor is activated repeatedly unless termination occurs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is empty or a box \(X^*\) satisfying \(X^{(0)}\cap S\subseteq X^*\) and \(C_i(X^*)=X^*\) for all \(i\).

notation.meaning: Sequence selecting the contractor activated at each iteration.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Solution preservation and the conditional common-fixed-point conclusion are plausible, but termination requires a precisely sourced finite-lattice, deterministic finite-precision, or other stabilization model. No authoritative propagation source is supplied.

children.title: Incremental Contractor Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Dependency-aware activation and reuse across shared variables and constraints.

children.title: Contractor Scheduling Policies
children.top_down_role: Queueing, ordering, fairness, and priority choices for contractor activation.

knowledge_statements.title: Contractor Scheduling Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies fair work-list activation for a finite family of variable-dependent contractors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a current box \(X\), contractors \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\), dependency sets \(D_i\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), initialize a queue with every index \(i\). Remove an index \(i\), set \(Y=C_i(X)\), and determine the changed coordinates \(J=\{j:Y_j\subsetneq X_j\}\). Replace \(X\) by \(Y\), and enqueue every \(\ell\) with \(D_\ell\cap J\ne\varnothing\). Stop when the queue is empty or \(X=\varnothing\). To retain completeness, the policy must be fair: every contractor whose relevant inputs change is eventually processed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fair work-list scheduler reactivates contractors affected by changed variable bounds and stops when the queue empties or infeasibility is detected.
assumptions_latex: Every contractor is solution-preserving.
Each dependency set contains every coordinate whose bound can affect its contractor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Queue exhaustion yields a dependency-stable box; emptiness certifies that the initial box contains no solution.

notation.meaning: Coordinates on which contractor i depends.
Coordinates tightened by the latest activation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The work-list algorithm fits the scheduling-policy leaf, but queue-exhaustion stability depends on complete dependency tracking and operational scheduling assumptions that need authoritative support.

children.title: Incremental Contractor Reuse
children.top_down_role: Reuse of prior contraction state after localized box or constraint changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Contractor Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the validity conditions for reusing cached contractor state after domain tightening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a contractor invocation on box \(X\) produce cached state \(\sigma(X)\), and let \(Y\subseteq X\) be a later box. Reusing that state is sound only if the incremental routine \(C^{\mathrm{inc}}(Y;\sigma(X))\) satisfies
\[Y\cap S\subseteq C^{\mathrm{inc}}(Y;\sigma(X))\subseteq Y.\]
A sufficient cache-validity discipline is that every cached enclosure, derivative bound, or logical support is either monotone-valid on all subboxes of \(X\) or recomputed whenever a coordinate on which it depends changes. Cached state may accelerate contraction but cannot replace this solution-preservation test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cached contractor information may be reused after tightening only when it remains valid on the subbox or is recomputed after relevant changes.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\subseteq X\) and \(S\) is the fixed target solution set.
Every cached item has a declared coordinate-dependency set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Valid reuse requires \(Y\cap S\subseteq C^{\mathrm{inc}}(Y;\sigma(X))\subseteq Y\).

notation.meaning: State cached from contractor processing on X.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The preservation condition is necessary for sound incremental reuse, but the proposed monotone-validity and dependency-triggered recomputation discipline is domain-specific and unsupported by a citation.

children.title: Dependency-Triggered Activation
children.top_down_role: Activation based on changed variables, affected expressions, or shared constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependency-Triggered Activation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work-list scheduling using explicit read–write dependencies among sound contractors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let contractors \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) act on a box \(X\), with read sets \(R_i\) and write sets \(W_i\). Initialize a queue with all indices. When \(i\) is removed, compute \(X^+=C_i(X)\). If \(X^+=\varnothing\), return infeasible. Otherwise, for every coordinate changed between \(X\) and \(X^+\), enqueue each \(j\) satisfying \(R_j\cap W_i\ne\varnothing\); then replace \(X\) by \(X^+\). Terminate when the queue is empty and return \(X\). Fair duplicate suppression is permitted, but every contractor invalidated by a relevant change must eventually execute.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run a contractor again whenever another contractor changes a variable it reads; stop at an empty box or when no dependency is pending.
assumptions_latex: \(C_i(X)\subseteq X\) for every \(i\) and box \(X\).
Each declared \(R_i\) and \(W_i\) conservatively contains the coordinates actually read and written.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X=\varnothing\) or every contractor affected by the final changes has been processed.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard event-driven constraint-propagation work-list algorithm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the scheduling leaf, and the dependency rule is plausible, but no inspectable contractor-scheduling citation is supplied. The statement also describes termination without hypotheses such as finite representable boxes, a stopping tolerance, or another condition preventing an infinite descending sequence.

children.title: Stale-State Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Correctness and effectiveness risks from incomplete invalidation or delayed reactivation.

knowledge_statements.title: Stale-State Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure caused by omitting reactivation after an input dependency changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(X=x\u007d\times Y\times Z\) with \(x=0\), \(Y=Z=[0,1]\), and the equality constraints \(x=y\) and \(y=z\). Let \(C_1\) replace \(Y\) by \(Y\capx\u007d\), and let \(C_2\) replace \(Z\) by \(Z\cap Y\). Executing \(C_2\) first leaves \(Z=[0,1]\); executing \(C_1\) next gives \(Y=0\u007d\). If the change of \(Y\) does not reactivate \(C_2\), scheduling terminates with \(Z=[0,1]\), although \(C_2\) would contract it to \(0\u007d\). Thus the returned state is stale and not a common contractor fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a contractor is not rerun after one of its inputs narrows, propagation may terminate at a box that is not a common fixed point.
assumptions_latex: The scheduler may execute \(C_2\) before \(C_1\).
A change to \(Y\) is not propagated to the dependency of \(C_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_2(X)\subsetneq X\) at the scheduler's purported terminal state.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit independently checkable propagation counterexample
published source for stale-state scheduling failure required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits the failure-boundary leaf and the intended example is mathematically credible. However, no published source is cited, and several encoded set expressions are malformed, including the box definition and singleton intervals.

children.title: Constraint-Propagation Contractors
children.top_down_role: Contractors derived from expression graphs and local consistency notions.

children.title: Forward-Backward-HC4 Propagation Family
children.top_down_role: Expression-tree propagation from variables to constraint images and back.

children.title: Forward–Backward Contractors
children.top_down_role: Expression-directed propagation between variable domains and constraint images.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward–Backward Contractors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-constraint contraction over a factorable expression and an interval target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a factorable constraint \(f(x)\in Y\) on an input box \(X\), represent \(f\) by an expression tree. In a forward sweep, assign each leaf its interval from \(X\) and each internal node a sound interval extension of its elementary operation. Intersect the root interval with \(Y\); return \(\varnothing\) if this intersection is empty. In a backward sweep, visit nodes toward the leaves and intersect every child interval with a sound inverse projection of its parent's current interval and the other child intervals. Intersect the resulting leaf intervals with \(X\) and return the contracted box \(C(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate an expression tree forward, restrict its root to the constraint target, then propagate sound inverse images backward to narrow variables.
assumptions_latex: Every forward operation encloses its real range.
Every backward projection contains all child values compatible with the current parent and sibling intervals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in X:f(x)\in Y\u007d\subseteq C(X)\subseteq X\).

notation.meaning: allowed interval at the expression root

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard forward evaluation and backward projection contractor

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and forward-backward description fit the leaf. An authoritative interval-constraint source is absent, and the soundness conclusion has malformed set-builder notation, so the exact supported formulation cannot yet be accepted.

children.title: HC4 Contractors
children.top_down_role: HC4-style consistency enforcement over decomposed expression structures.

knowledge_statements.title: HC4 Contractors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: HC4Revise contraction for one admissible expression-tree constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an admissible expression tree for \(f(x)=0\) and a box \(X\), HC4Revise first performs a bottom-up interval evaluation of every node. It intersects the root interval with \(0\u007d\), returning \(\varnothing\) if the intersection is empty. It then performs one top-down sweep of sound inverse projections, intersecting each node interval with values compatible with its parent and siblings. Repeated occurrences of a variable are finally intersected together with its component of \(X\). For several constraints, HC4 repeatedly schedules their HC4Revise operators until a stopping tolerance, an empty box, or a propagation fixed point is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: HC4 applies one forward and one backward tree sweep per constraint, then schedules constraints repeatedly to propagate their contractions.
assumptions_latex: The expression is composed of elementary operations having inclusion-isotonic interval extensions and sound inverse projections.
Undefined operation domains are intersected with their admissible real domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in X:f(x)=0\u007d\subseteq \operatorname{HC4Revise}(X)\subseteq X\).
review_flags: original HC4 source and precise admissibility conditions required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits HC4 Contractors, but the original or an authoritative HC4 source with precise admissibility and inverse-projection conditions is required. The singleton and solution-set notation is also malformed.

children.title: Expression-Tree Propagation
children.top_down_role: Propagation organization induced by expression-tree topology and intermediate nodes.

knowledge_statements.title: Expression-Tree Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary-variable representation underlying tree-based interval propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a factorable expression be represented by a rooted tree with leaves labeled by variables or constants and internal nodes labeled by elementary operations. Associate an auxiliary variable \(v_t\) with every node \(t\). For an internal node with children \(t_1,\ldots,t_k\) and operation \(\phi_t\), impose \(v_t=\phi_t(v_{t_1},\ldots,v_{t_k})\); identify each variable leaf with its component of \(x\), and restrict the root variable to the constraint target. The original constraint and this auxiliary system have the same projection onto \(x\). Local interval contractors on the node equations therefore yield a sound contractor for the original constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expression tree becomes an equivalent auxiliary-variable system; propagating its node equations and projecting to original variables gives sound contraction.
assumptions_latex: Each occurrence in the syntactic expression is represented by one tree leaf.
All auxiliary node equations use the same real operation domains as the original expression.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x:f(x)\in Y\u007d=\operatorname{proj}_x(x,v):v_t=\phi_t(v_{t_1},\ldots,v_{t_k}),\ v_{\mathrm{root}}\in Y\).

notation.meaning: auxiliary value of expression-tree node t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard auxiliary-variable semantics of expression trees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind matches the expression-tree leaf, and the auxiliary-variable semantics are standard. No inspectable propagation citation is supplied, and the projection equality omits proper set braces around both sets.

children.title: Shared-Subexpression Effects
children.top_down_role: Dependency, reuse, and contraction effects arising from repeated expression components.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Subexpression Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependency loss when repeated occurrences are propagated as independent interval quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Tree-based interval evaluation generally loses correlations between repeated occurrences. For \(X=[-1,1]\) and \(f(x)=x-x\), treating the two leaves independently gives \(f(X)=X-X=[-2,2]\), whereas the exact range is \(0\u007d\). Consequently, a forward–backward contractor based only on independent occurrence intervals need not detect targets disjoint from \(0\u007d\) whenever they intersect \([-2,2]\). Preserving a shared node in a directed acyclic graph, introducing an equality linking duplicated auxiliaries, or simplifying the expression can recover dependency information; merely reusing the same numerical interval at both leaves does not guarantee recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent interval treatment of repeated subexpressions loses correlation and can weaken contraction; explicit sharing, equality links, or simplification may restore it.
assumptions_latex: Ordinary interval arithmetic treats the two occurrences in \(x-x\) independently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{range}(x-x,X)=0\u007d\subsetneq[-2,2]=X-X\).

notation.meaning: interval domain of the shared variable

review_flags: source specifically addressing shared-subexpression propagation required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and dependency example fit the leaf. A source specifically supporting the propagation consequences is missing, singleton notation is malformed, and the statement that DAG sharing or equality links can recover dependency information needs precise conditions because local interval propagation need not recover the exact correlation.

children.title: Hull-Consistency Contractors
children.top_down_role: Contraction organized around hull consistency of projected constraint solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Hull-Consistency Contractors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact coordinate-projection hull consistency for a single constraint over a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=x\in X:g(x)\in Y\), where \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_n\) is a box. The constraint is hull consistent on \(X\) when, for every coordinate \(i\), \(X_i=\operatorname{hull}(\operatorname{proj}_i S)\). Its ideal hull-consistency contractor is \(C_H(X)=\prod_{i=1}^n\operatorname{hull}(\operatorname{proj}_i S)\), with \(C_H(X)=\varnothing\) if \(S=\varnothing\). A computable hull-consistency contractor may return an outer enclosure of \(C_H(X)\), but must remain contracting and retain every point of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hull consistency makes each coordinate interval the interval hull of that coordinate’s feasible projection; practical contractors safely enclose this ideal contraction.
assumptions_latex: \(X_i\) and \(Y\) are closed real intervals.
The interval hull of an empty projection is interpreted as empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\subseteq C_H(X)\subseteq X\).

notation.meaning: smallest closed interval containing a set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact projection-hull definition of hull consistency
terminology varies between hull consistency and hull(2B) consistency; source required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the topic, but the feasible set S is not written with set-builder braces. An authoritative locator is also needed to distinguish exact hull consistency from hull or 2B-consistency terminology and to support the stated practical-contractor convention.

children.title: Box-Consistency Contractors
children.top_down_role: Coordinatewise consistency enforced through interval root and shaving tests.

knowledge_statements.title: Box-Consistency Contractors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise interval consistency defined through univariate inclusion tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an equation \(f(x)=0\) on \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_n\), fix coordinate \(i\) and define the interval-valued univariate map \(F_i(t)=f(X_1,\ldots,X_{i-1},t,X_{i+1},\ldots,X_n)\) using a sound interval extension. The equation is box consistent in coordinate \(i\) when the left and right endpoints of \(X_i\) cannot be removed by the prescribed canonical-interval tests \(0\in F_i(I)\). A box-consistency contractor applies interval root isolation or shaving to delete endpoint slices failing these tests, repeats over coordinates, and returns a contracting box containing every zero in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Box consistency shaves coordinate endpoints whose univariate interval tests cannot contain zero, while preserving all solutions of the full equation.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) has a sound interval extension.
Canonical endpoint intervals and outward rounding are fixed by the interval arithmetic implementation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in X:f(x)=0\u007d\subseteq C_B(X)\subseteq X\).

notation.meaning: univariate interval inclusion map for coordinate i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard coordinate shaving interpretation of box consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the topic, but 'prescribed canonical-interval tests' does not explicitly define the canonical endpoint intervals or the exact endpoint condition. Since variants are implementation-sensitive and no authoritative locator is supplied, the mathematical definition remains unreliable; the conclusion also has malformed set-builder notation.

children.title: Linear-Relaxation Contractors
children.top_down_role: Validated contraction through linear outer approximations.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Relaxation Contractors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validated box contraction using a certified linear outer approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a box \(X\) and constraints with feasible set \(S\cap X\), construct a polyhedron \(P_X=x:Ax\le b\) using outward-rounded coefficients such that \(S\cap X\subseteq P_X\cap X\). If \(P_X\cap X=\varnothing\) is certified, return \(\varnothing\). Otherwise, for each coordinate solve validated linear programs for lower and upper bounds of \(x_i\) over \(P_X\cap X\), round the lower optimum downward and the upper optimum upward, and intersect these bounds with \(X_i\). Return the product box \(C_L(X)\). Any safely weaker LP bounds remain valid, although they may contract less.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer-approximate nonlinear feasibility by certified linear inequalities, then solve coordinate LPs to narrow the box without losing feasible points.
assumptions_latex: \(S\cap X\subseteq P_X\cap X\).
LP infeasibility and objective bounds are certified with directed rounding or exact verification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\cap X\subseteq C_L(X)\subseteq X\).

notation.meaning: certified polyhedral outer approximation on X

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the linear-relaxation contractor topic and the outer-approximation logic is sound in outline. No validated linear-relaxation source is cited, and the definition of P_X omits set-builder braces.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Equation Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval Newton existence and uniqueness certificate for a square nonlinear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable on a box \(X\), choose \(x_0\in X\), and let \([J_F](X)\) enclose every Jacobian on \(X\). Define an interval Newton image \(N(X)=x_0-[J_F](X)^{-1}F(x_0)\), interpreting the interval linear solve by a verified enclosure. If \(N(X)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(X)\), then \(X\) contains exactly one zero of \(F\). If \(N(X)\cap X=\varnothing\), then \(X\) contains no zero. Otherwise, replacing \(X\) by \(X\cap N(X)\) is a sound contraction whenever the verified interval Newton inclusion is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A verified interval Newton image strictly inside a box certifies one root; disjointness excludes roots, and intersection safely contracts an undecided box.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on an open set containing \(X\).
The interval Jacobian and interval linear solve are inclusion-valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(X)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(X)\Rightarrow\exists!x^*\in X:F(x^*)=0\), and \(N(X)\cap X=\varnothing\Rightarrow F^{-1}(0)\cap X=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: interval enclosure of the Jacobian over X

children.title: Unconstrained Stationarity Systems
children.top_down_role: Critical-point systems for smooth bound-constrained optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Stationarity Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity system for smooth optimization over a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of the box \(B=[\ell,u]\). A local minimizer \(x^*\in B\) satisfies, for each coordinate \(i\), \(\partial_i f(x^*)=0\) when \(\ell_i<x_i^*<u_i\), \(\partial_i f(x^*)\ge0\) when \(x_i^*=\ell_i<u_i\), and \(\partial_i f(x^*)\le0\) when \(x_i^*=u_i>\ell_i\). Equivalently, there exist multipliers \(\lambda^L,\lambda^U\ge0\) satisfying \(\nabla f(x^*)-\lambda^L+\lambda^U=0\), \(\lambda_i^L(x_i^*-\ell_i)=0\), and \(\lambda_i^U(u_i-x_i^*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth box-constrained local minimizer satisfies gradient balance, multiplier nonnegativity, and complementarity with its active lower and upper bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^1\) on a neighborhood of \(B\).
\(B\) is nonempty and \(\ell_i<u_i\) for every coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\text{ locally minimizes }f\text{ on }B\Rightarrow(x^*,\lambda^L,\lambda^U)\text{ satisfies the displayed stationarity system}.\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard KKT system for box constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the stationarity-system leaf, and the displayed bound-constrained first-order conditions have the correct signs under the stated nondegenerate bounds. An authoritative optimality-conditions section, theorem, or page locator is still required.

children.title: Constrained Optimality Systems
children.top_down_role: Multiplier-based systems for constrained optimizer verification.

knowledge_statements.title: Constrained Optimality Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT equation–complementarity interface for verified constrained optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le0\), with continuously differentiable data. If \(x^*\) is a local minimizer and the linear-independence constraint qualification holds for equality gradients and active inequality gradients, then there exist \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\ge0\) such that \(\nabla f(x^*)+J_h(x^*)^\mathsf{T}\lambda+J_g(x^*)^\mathsf{T}\mu=0\), \(h(x^*)=0\), \(g(x^*)\le0\), and \(\mu_jg_j(x^*)=0\) for every \(j\). Fixing a candidate active set converts these conditions into a square equality system suitable for interval Newton verification, followed by sign and inactivity checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under LICQ, a constrained local minimizer satisfies KKT stationarity, feasibility, multiplier signs, and complementarity; active-set choices yield systems for interval verification.
assumptions_latex: \(f,h,g\) are continuously differentiable near \(x^*\).
LICQ holds at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\text{ locally minimizes }f\Rightarrow\exists(\lambda,\mu)\text{ satisfying the displayed KKT conditions}.\)

children.title: Direct Interval Newton Methods
children.top_down_role: Direct enclosure of Newton images through validated interval linear solves.

assumptions_latex: \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuously differentiable on an open set containing the box \(X\subset D\).
\(\hat x\in X\), and \(J(X)\) encloses \(F'(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
A validated interval linear solver returns a box \(Y\) containing every \(y\) satisfying \(Ay=F(\hat x)\) for some \(A\in J(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X^+=X\cap N(X)\) is a validated contraction; emptiness excludes a zero, while strict interior inclusion certifies a unique zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical square-system interval Newton step using a validated direct interval linear solve.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute an interval enclosure \(Y\) of the united solution set of \(Ay=F(\hat x)\) with \(A\in J(X)\), and define \[N(X)=\hat x-Y,\qquad X^+=X\cap N(X).\] Every zero of \(F\) in \(X\) belongs to \(X^+\). Hence \(X^+=\varnothing\) proves that \(X\) contains no zero. Under the standard interval Newton regularity conditions, \(N(X)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(X)\) proves that \(F\) has exactly one zero in \(X\). Otherwise return \(X^+\) for further contraction or subdivision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enclose the solutions of the interval Newton linear system, intersect its translated image with the box, and use emptiness or strict interior inclusion as validated certificates.
knowledge_statements.title: Direct Interval Newton Methods

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Direct interval Newton iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Box contraction through an enclosure of the solution of the interval Newton linear equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $X_0:=X$. For $n=0,1,2,\ldots$, choose $x_n\in X_n$, determine a superbox $Z_{n+1}$ of a solution $Y_{n+1}$ of the interval linear equation $J(X_n)(x_n-Y)=\phi(x_n)$, and set $X_{n+1}:=Z_{n+1}\cap X_n$. One interval Newton iteration is the execution of these three operations for a fixed $n$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize the current box as X. At each iteration, select a point in the current box, enclose a solution of the associated interval linear equation in a superbox, and intersect that superbox with the current box.
assumptions_latex: X_0=X
n\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}
x_n\in X_n
Y_{n+1}\subseteq Z_{n+1}
J(X_n)(x_n-Y_{n+1})=\phi(x_n)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_{n+1}=Z_{n+1}\cap X_n\subseteq X_n

children.title: Hansen–Sengupta Methods
children.top_down_role: Preconditioned interval Gauss–Seidel contraction and verification.

assumptions_latex: \(F\), \(X\), \(\hat x\), and \(J(X)\) satisfy the square-system interval Newton assumptions.
\(C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular, usually approximating \(\operatorname{mid}(J(X))^{-1}\).
Interval Gauss–Seidel operations use outward rounding and intersect each updated component with \(X-\hat x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Hansen–Sengupta image contracts \(X\); emptiness excludes zeros, and strict interior inclusion verifies a unique zero under regularity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preconditioned interval Gauss–Seidel form for square nonlinear systems.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(B=CJ(X)\), \(b=-CF(\hat x)\), and \(Z=X-\hat x\). Starting from \(Z\), perform one outward-rounded interval Gauss–Seidel sweep on \(Bz=b\), intersecting each newly computed coordinate with its current coordinate interval; denote the result by \(\Gamma(B,b,Z)\). Define \[H(X)=\hat x+\Gamma(B,b,Z),\qquad X^+=X\cap H(X).\] Every zero of \(F\) in \(X\) remains in \(X^+\). Thus \(X^+=\varnothing\) excludes zeros, while \(H(X)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(X)\), with the usual regularity hypotheses, certifies existence and uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precondition the interval Newton equation, apply an interval Gauss–Seidel sweep, and interpret empty or strictly interior images as exclusion or uniqueness certificates.
knowledge_statements.title: Hansen–Sengupta Methods

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic content matches Hansen–Sengupta methods, but "square-system interval Newton assumptions" and "usual regularity hypotheses" are not explicit enough to support the existence-and-uniqueness certificate. A Hansen–Sengupta-specific theorem or section locator is required.

children.title: Krawczyk Operator Methods
children.top_down_role: Point-preconditioned fixed-point verification operators.

assumptions_latex: \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuously differentiable around the box \(X\subset D\).
\(\hat x\in X\), and \(J(X)\) encloses every Jacobian on \(X\).
\(C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is a nonsingular point preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K(X)\cap X\) retains all zeros; disjointness excludes zeros and strict self-inclusion certifies a unique zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical point-preconditioned Krawczyk certificate for a square nonlinear system.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the Krawczyk image by \[K(X)=\hat x-CF(\hat x)+\bigl(I-CJ(X)\bigr)(X-\hat x).\] Every zero of \(F\) lying in \(X\) also lies in \(K(X)\cap X\). Consequently, \(K(X)\cap X=\varnothing\) certifies that \(X\) contains no zero. If \(K(X)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(X)\), then the standard Krawczyk theorem certifies that \(X\) contains a zero and that this zero is unique in \(X\). When neither test succeeds, \(K(X)\cap X\) is a validated contracted box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Krawczyk operator combines a point inverse with an interval Jacobian remainder; disjointness excludes roots, while strict self-inclusion certifies one unique root.
knowledge_statements.title: Krawczyk Operator Methods

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

children.title: Slope-Based Interval Newton Methods
children.top_down_role: Newton operators using slope enclosures in place of ordinary derivative intervals.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuous on the box \(X\), and \(\hat x\in X\).
For every \(x\in X\), a slope matrix \(S(x,\hat x)\) satisfies \(F(x)-F(\hat x)=S(x,\hat x)(x-\hat x)\).
The interval matrix \(S(X,\hat x)\) encloses all such slope matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing the interval Jacobian by a valid slope enclosure preserves interval Newton exclusion and strict-inclusion verification.

notation.meaning: Slope enclosure relative to the center

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slope-enclosure variant of direct interval Newton for potentially nondifferentiable or dependency-sensitive formulations.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Use a validated interval linear solver to enclose by \(Y_S\) every solution \(y\) of \(Ay=F(\hat x)\) with \(A\in S(X,\hat x)\), and set \[N_S(X)=\hat x-Y_S,
\qquad X^+=X\cap N_S(X).\] The slope identity implies that every zero of \(F\) in \(X\) belongs to \(X^+\). Therefore \(X^+=\varnothing\) excludes zeros. Subject to the corresponding nonsingularity and interval Newton regularity assumptions, \(N_S(X)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(X)\) certifies existence and uniqueness of a zero in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slope enclosure can replace the derivative enclosure in interval Newton while retaining validated contraction, exclusion, and strict-inclusion verification.
knowledge_statements.title: Slope-Based Interval Newton Methods

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

However, the strict-inclusion existence-and-uniqueness conclusion is qualified only by unspecified "corresponding" regularity assumptions, and the cited locator is not slope-specific.

children.title: Midpoint-Inverse Preconditioning
children.top_down_role: Point-matrix preconditioning based on a representative Jacobian.

assumptions_latex: \(J(X)\in\mathbb{IR}^{n\times n}\) is an interval Jacobian enclosure.
Its midpoint matrix \(M=\operatorname{mid}(J(X))\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The midpoint-inverse preconditioner is \(C=M^{-1}\), and the midpoint of the preconditioned interval matrix equals \(I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard point preconditioner formed from the inverse of a representative interval Jacobian midpoint.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an interval matrix \(J(X)\) whose midpoint \(M=\operatorname{mid}(J(X))\) is nonsingular, midpoint-inverse preconditioning selects the point matrix \[C=M^{-1}.\] The interval Newton linear system is left-preconditioned by \(C\), replacing \(J(X)y=F(\hat x)\) by \(CJ(X)y=CF(\hat x)\). Because multiplication by a point matrix commutes with taking interval midpoints, \[\operatorname{mid}\bigl(CJ(X)\bigr)=CM=I.\] Thus the transformed interval matrix is centered at the identity, although its radius and resulting contraction quality need not be minimal among admissible preconditioners.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invert the midpoint Jacobian and use it as a point left preconditioner, centering the transformed interval matrix at the identity.
knowledge_statements.title: Midpoint-Inverse Preconditioning

children.title: Optimal Preconditioner Selection
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary optimization criteria for choosing interval Newton preconditioners.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is a nonempty admissible set of point preconditioners.
\(\Phi:\mathcal C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is a specified contraction, width, or verification surrogate.
The minimum of \(\Phi\) over \(\mathcal C\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A preconditioner is optimal only relative to the declared pair \((\mathcal C,\Phi)\), namely when it belongs to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{C\in\mathcal C}\Phi(C)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: optimality must be defined relative to an admissible set and explicit objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion-relative definition; it does not assert a universally optimal interval Newton preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an admissible class \(\mathcal C\) and a declared surrogate \(\Phi\), an optimal preconditioner is any matrix \[C^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{C\in\mathcal C}\Phi(C).\] Typical surrogates measure the width of \(CJ(X)\), a norm bound for \(I-CJ(X)\), or the predicted width of a resulting contractor image. The optimization problem must specify normalization or boundedness constraints whenever scaling \(C\) can change \(\Phi\) without changing the underlying linear equations. Optimality is therefore relative to \(\mathcal C\), \(\Phi\), and the chosen interval evaluation; it does not imply best realized contraction for every box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal preconditioner minimizes a specified contraction surrogate over an explicitly constrained class; no matrix is universally optimal independently of that criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal Preconditioner Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Criterion-relative argmin optimality is coherent and the definition content kind fits the leaf. However, the interval-specific claims about representative surrogates, normalization, interval evaluation, and realized contractor quality have no inspectable source beyond a general standard-field rationale.

children.title: LP-Based Preconditioner Selection
children.top_down_role: Linear-programming formulations for preconditioner choice or refinement.

assumptions_latex: The admissible preconditioners have an affine parametrization \(C(c)=C_0+\sum_{k=1}^m c_kC_k\).
The surrogate has the polyhedral form \(\Phi(c)=\max_{1\le r\le q}(a_r^\top c+b_r)\).
Additional admissibility restrictions are linear inequalities \(Gc\le h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimizing the polyhedral surrogate is equivalent to an epigraph linear program, and its optimizer defines the selected preconditioner.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: epigraph reformulation of a finite maximum of affine functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP reduction for polyhedral preconditioner objectives, not for arbitrary nonlinear contraction measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form the epigraph linear program \[\min_{c,t}\ t\quad\text{subject to}\quad a_r^\top c+b_r\le t\ \text{for }r=1,\ldots,q,\qquad Gc\le h.\] If the program is feasible and attains an optimizer \((c^\star,t^\star)\), return \(C(c^\star)\). The epigraph constraints imply \(t\ge\Phi(c)\), while at an optimum \(t^\star=\Phi(c^\star)\); hence the returned matrix minimizes the stated polyhedral surrogate over the admissible affine family. Interval coefficients used to construct the data must first be replaced by verified deterministic bounds appropriate to the chosen surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the selection surrogate is a maximum of affine functions, introduce an epigraph variable and solve the resulting constrained linear program.
knowledge_statements.title: LP-Based Preconditioner Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The epigraph LP reformulation is correct for the explicitly assumed finite maximum of affine functions, and algorithm is the appropriate content kind. The claims about constructing verified deterministic LP data from interval coefficients require an interval-preconditioning or verified-optimization source with a specific locator.

children.title: Selection-Cost Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Balance between auxiliary optimization expense and subsequent contraction quality.

assumptions_latex: A baseline method costs \(T_0\) per contractor call and has expected contraction factor \(q_0\in(0,1)\).
A selected preconditioner costs \(T_{\mathrm{sel}}\) once, \(T_C\) per call, and has expected factor \(q_C\in(0,1)\).
The same preconditioner is reused for \(m\ge1\) comparable calls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Selection is cost-favorable exactly when \(T_{\mathrm{sel}}+mT_C<mT_0\), provided the required contraction quality is met.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: amortized-cost comparison under an explicit reuse model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic amortized-cost condition under a simplified repeated-call model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an acceptable contraction threshold \(\bar q\in(0,1)\). The selected preconditioner is preferable in the stated cost model precisely when \[q_C\le\bar q,
\qquad T_{\mathrm{sel}}+mT_C<mT_0.\] If \(T_0>T_C\), the cost inequality is equivalent to \[m>\frac{T_{\mathrm{sel}}}{T_0-T_C}.\] If \(T_0\le T_C\), no positive reuse count amortizes the selection cost under this model. The comparison is conditional on the predicted factors and timings being representative; it does not establish a machine-independent advantage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expensive selection pays off only when its one-time cost is amortized across enough calls while the chosen preconditioner meets the required contraction quality.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Cost Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The amortized timing inequality is algebraically correct under the simplified model, but the conclusion_latex calls it an exact preference condition without including the required contraction threshold that appears in the statement. The interpretation of expected contraction factors and representative timings also lacks an inspectable source.

children.title: Optimization-Based Selection Failures
children.top_down_role: Degeneracy, instability, or excessive overhead in auxiliary selection models.

assumptions_latex: \(J\in\mathbb{IR}^{n\times n}\) contains a singular point matrix \(A\in J\).
\(C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is any nonsingular point preconditioner.
\(\|\cdot\|\) is any induced matrix norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No point preconditioner can satisfy the uniform contraction bound \(\sup_{B\in J}\|I-CB\|<1\) when \(J\) contains a singular matrix.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a matrix within induced-norm distance below one from identity is nonsingular
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp obstruction for uniform identity-centered norm contraction over an interval matrix family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(J\in\mathbb{IR}^{n\times n}\) contains a singular matrix, then every nonsingular point preconditioner \(C\in\operatorname{GL}(n)\) satisfies \[\sup_{B\in J}\|I-CB\|\ge 1.\] Consequently, \[\inf_{C\in\operatorname{GL}(n)}\sup_{B\in J}\|I-CB\|\ge 1.\] Thus optimization over nonsingular point preconditioners cannot produce a uniform identity-centered induced-norm contraction factor strictly below one for such an interval family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the interval matrix contains a singular member, no nonsingular point preconditioner can make every preconditioned member uniformly closer than one to the identity.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-Based Selection Failures

children.title: Interval Linear-System Transformations
children.top_down_role: Structural transformations supporting stable interval linear contraction.

children.title: Interval System Scaling
children.top_down_role: Row, column, and variable scaling for conditioning interval linear systems.

assumptions_latex: \(Ax=b\) denotes the family with \(A\in\mathbf A\) and \(b\in\mathbf b\).
\(D_r,D_c\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) are nonsingular diagonal point matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Two-sided point scaling preserves the united solution set under the bijection \(x=D_cz\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: invertible point changes of variables preserve each member system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact solution-set equivalence for nonsingular point diagonal scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the scaled interval system by \[\widetilde{\mathbf A}=D_r\mathbf A D_c,
\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf b}=D_r\mathbf b,
\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf A}z=\widetilde{\mathbf b}.\] Its united solution set satisfies \[\Sigma(\widetilde{\mathbf A},\widetilde{\mathbf b})=D_c^{-1}\Sigma(\mathbf A,\mathbf b),\] where \(\Sigma(\mathbf A,\mathbf b)=\{x:Ax=b\text{ for some }A\in\mathbf A,
 b\in\mathbf b\}\). Thus \(x=D_cz\) maps scaled solutions bijectively to original solutions. Scaling may alter interval widths, conditioning bounds, and elimination behavior, but not the represented exact family when the scaling matrices are point and nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsingular point row and column scalings transform an interval linear system without changing its exact solution family, after the corresponding variable map.
knowledge_statements.title: Interval System Scaling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-sided point-scaling equivalence is mathematically plausible and representation is the correct content kind. However, the interval-family interpretation and united-solution-set identity have no specific inspectable source, despite the record explicitly flagging that requirement.

children.title: Interval System Permutation
children.top_down_role: Equation or variable reorderings supporting favorable interval linear structure.

assumptions_latex: \(Ax=b\) ranges over \(A\in\mathbf A\) and \(b\in\mathbf b\).
\(P,Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) are permutation matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Row and column permutations preserve the united solution set up to the coordinate bijection \(x=Qz\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: permutation matrices are invertible coordinate transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence of interval system families under fixed row and column permutations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Form the permuted interval system \[\widetilde{\mathbf A}=P\mathbf A Q,
\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf b}=P\mathbf b,
\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf A}z=\widetilde{\mathbf b}.\] Because \(P^{-1}=P^\top\) and \(Q^{-1}=Q^\top\), its united solution set obeys \[\Sigma(\widetilde{\mathbf A},\widetilde{\mathbf b})=Q^\top\Sigma(\mathbf A,
\mathbf b).\] Hence \(x=Qz\) recovers exactly the solutions of the original family. Row permutation changes equation order, and column permutation changes variable order; either can improve the availability and quality of interval pivots without changing feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed row and column permutations merely reorder equations and variables, preserving the interval system's exact solution family through a coordinate permutation.
knowledge_statements.title: Interval System Permutation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The permutation identities are internally consistent and representation fits the exact leaf. A specific interval-linear-system source is still required to support the united-solution-set formulation and the claim concerning pivot quality.

children.title: Interval Pivoting Strategies
children.top_down_role: Pivot choices for stable elimination or preconditioned interval contraction.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathbf A z=\mathbf b\) is a square interval linear system processed with outward rounding.
At elimination stage \(k\), row and column permutations may be applied to the active submatrix.
A usable pivot interval \(\mathbf p\) must satisfy \(0\notin\mathbf p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every completed outward-rounded elimination step encloses the transformed system; absence of a nonzero pivot requires subdivision or a different verified solver.

notation.meaning: Magnitude lower bound of an interval

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: interval division is valid only when the divisor excludes zero
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validated pivot selection for interval Gaussian elimination, with explicit zero-containing-pivot failure handling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At stage \(k\), choose an active entry \(\mathbf a_{ij}\) with \(0\notin\mathbf a_{ij}\), preferably maximizing a declared score such as \(\operatorname{mig}(\mathbf a_{ij})\). Permute it to position \((k,k)\), set \(\mathbf p=\mathbf a_{kk}\), and perform the interval elimination updates \[\mathbf m_{ik}=\mathbf a_{ik}/\mathbf p,
\qquad \mathbf a_{ij}\leftarrow\mathbf a_{ij}-\mathbf m_{ik}\mathbf a_{kj},
\qquad \mathbf b_i\leftarrow\mathbf b_i-\mathbf m_{ik}\mathbf b_k\] with outward rounding. Continue through all stages and apply verified back substitution. If every candidate pivot contains zero, stop and return an unresolved status, subdivision request, or alternative verified solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a pivot interval excluding zero, permute it into place, eliminate with outward rounding, and stop safely when no valid pivot exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Interval Pivoting Strategies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm belongs in the interval pivoting container and correctly prevents division by a zero-containing pivot. The broader claim that the completed interval elimination and back-substitution enclose the relevant transformed system depends on the precise verified elimination semantics and dependency handling, for which no source or theorem locator is supplied.

children.title: Transformation Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditioning and enclosure risks introduced by unsuitable structural transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Transformation Stability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundaries for equivalence and reliable enclosure under left preconditioning of an interval Newton system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^n\), and let \(P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be a point preconditioner. If \(P\) is nonsingular, then \(Ax=b\) and \(PAx=Pb\) have exactly the same solutions. This equivalence fails when \(P\) is singular. For nonsingular \(P\), perturbations satisfy \[\|\delta x\|\leq \|(PA)^{-1}\|\bigl(\|\delta(Pb)\|+\|\delta(PA)\|\,\|x\|\bigr).\] Consequently, interval transformation is verification-stable only while transformed rounding and enclosure errors remain smaller than the strict inclusion or exclusion margin; near singularity of \(PA\) can erase that margin without changing the exact solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsingular preconditioning preserves exact solutions, but poor transformed conditioning can amplify enclosure error enough to destroy an interval verification test.
assumptions_latex: \(A,P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^n\).
The displayed perturbation bound uses a subordinate matrix norm and nonsingular \(PA\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact equivalence requires nonsingular \(P\); numerical certification additionally requires transformed errors below the verification margin.

notation.meaning: Perturbations introduced in the transformed system.
A subordinate vector or matrix norm.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited locator does not presently establish the preconditioning boundary or perturbation formula. The displayed bound omits the conditions or higher-order term needed for coefficient perturbations, and singular P does not invariably change a particular solution set; rather, it removes the general equivalence guarantee.

children.title: Interval Newton Certification Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Logical outcomes supplied by interval Newton and related fixed-point operators.

children.title: Interval Newton Exclusion
children.top_down_role: Certified absence of relevant roots from a box.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Newton Exclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Root exclusion using the fundamental containment property of an interval Newton image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable, let \(X\subset D\) be a box, choose \(\hat x\in X\), and let \(J(X)\) contain every Jacobian \(F'(x)\) for \(x\in X\). Define an interval Newton enclosure \(N(\hat x,X)\) to contain every \(y\) satisfying \(A(y-\hat x)=-F(\hat x)\) for some \(A\in J(X)\). Every zero of \(F\) in \(X\) belongs to \(N(\hat x,X)\cap X\). Hence \[N(\hat x,X)\cap X=\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 0\notin F(X)\text{ as an attained value},\] so \(X\) contains no zero of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the interval Newton image does not intersect the original box, the box contains no root.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on a domain containing \(X\).
\(J(X)\) encloses \(F'(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
\(N(\hat x,X)\) is an outward-rounded enclosure of all stated linear-system solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\hat x,X)\cap X=\varnothing\) certifies that \(F(x)\neq0\) for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: Interval enclosure of the Jacobian on the box.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

children.title: Interval Newton Existence
children.top_down_role: Certified existence of a root in a designated region.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Newton Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional interval Newton inclusion theorem, stated for a strictly interior image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable, let \(X\subset D\) be a compact box, and choose \(\hat x\in X\). Let \(J(X)\) enclose \(F'(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), and let \(N(\hat x,X)\) be an outward-rounded interval Newton enclosure of all solutions of \(A(y-\hat x)=-F(\hat x)\) with \(A\in J(X)\). If \[N(\hat x,X)\subseteq\operatorname{int}X,\] then there exists \(x^*\in\operatorname{int}X\) such that \(F(x^*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict containment of the interval Newton image in the box certifies existence of a root in the box interior.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on a domain containing the compact box \(X\).
\(J(X)\) encloses all Jacobians on \(X\).
The interval Newton linear-system enclosure is well defined and outward rounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\hat x,X)\subseteq\operatorname{int}X\) implies existence of \(x^*\in\operatorname{int}X\) with \(F(x^*)=0\).

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

children.title: Interval Newton Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Certified isolation of a unique root.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Newton Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness in the tested box under strict interval Newton inclusion and regularity of the interval Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable, let \(X\subset D\) be a compact box, and choose \(\hat x\in X\). Suppose \(J(X)\) encloses every \(F'(x)\), every matrix \(A\in J(X)\) is nonsingular, and the interval Newton image satisfies \[N(\hat x,X)\subseteq\operatorname{int}X.\] Then \(F\) has exactly one zero \(x^*\) in \(X\). In particular, the strict inclusion supplies existence, while regularity of \(J(X)\) prevents two distinct zeros in the box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict Newton inclusion together with nonsingularity of every enclosed Jacobian certifies exactly one root in the box.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on a domain containing \(X\).
\(J(X)\) encloses all Jacobians on \(X\) and is regular.
\(N(\hat x,X)\subseteq\operatorname{int}X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists exactly one \(x^*\in X\) satisfying \(F(x^*)=0\).

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

children.title: Interval Newton Contraction Without Verification
children.top_down_role: Useful domain reduction when existence or uniqueness remains unresolved.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Newton Contraction Without Verification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe box reduction when neither exclusion nor an interior-inclusion certificate succeeds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the interval Newton containment assumptions, define \(X^+=X\cap N(\hat x,X)\). Every zero \(x^*\in X\) satisfies \(x^*\in X^+\). Thus, if \(\varnothing\neq X^+\subsetneq X\), replacing \(X\) by \(X^+\) is a root-preserving contraction. When \(N(\hat x,X)\not\subseteq\operatorname{int}X\), this contraction alone certifies neither existence nor uniqueness: \(X^+\) may be nonempty even though \(F\) has no zero in \(X\), or it may contain several zeros.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting with the Newton image safely removes root-free portions, but a nonempty proper contraction alone proves neither existence nor uniqueness.
assumptions_latex: Every zero of \(F\) in \(X\) is contained in the outward-rounded image \(N(\hat x,X)\).
\(X^+=X\cap N(\hat x,X)\) is computed by outward-rounded interval intersection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X^+\subsetneq X\) preserves every root in \(X\), but without strict interior inclusion it is not a root-verification certificate.
